INCREASES IN OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1947 AND 1949
speechtext: Were the increases in old age pensions in 1947 and 1949 granted as a result of representations made by the government of the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: INCREASES IN OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1947 AND 1949
speechtext:
No. The increases in old age pensions from $25 to $30 in 1947, and $30 to $40 in 1949, were granted as a result of action taken by the parliament of Canada to amend the federal Old Age Pensions Act. Following the passage by the parliament of Canada of
legislation authorizing these increases in pension, the government of the province of Quebec together with the other provinces of Canada accepted the offer contained in the federal legislation, and put into effect the increases authorized by the amending federal law.
The government of the province of Quebec was notified in advance of the federal government's intention to introduce these amendments in 1947 and 1949, but at no time were representations received from the government of the province of Quebec that the amount of pension should be increased.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) asked for more definite information as to the location of the new scallop bed recently discovered in the Northumberland strait area. This scallop bed lies approximately nine and one-half sea miles east, northeast, (magnetic) off the Richibucto harbour buoy. It runs northeast and southwest, is roughly oval in shape and approximately one and one-half miles long and one-half mile wide.
Using the British Admiralty chart No. 2034 or the U.S. navy hydrographic office chart No. 1066 for plotting, the positions are as follows:
Southern end 46 deg. 51' 00" N. lat.
64 deg. 37' 00" W. long.
Northern end 46 deg. 51' 30" N. lat.
64 deg. 36' 00" W. long.
The bed is marked at each end by staff buoys flying red and white flags.
There was a biological bulletin issued on June 25 regarding this bed, and I might also add that an item about its discovery appeared in Trade News of May.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. 393, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to make any statement on section 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, it was my intention to do so. As I have already said, this bill follows the form of all previous bills on representation, with the exception of a certain number of incidental amendments having to do with the elections act and the controverted elections act which will be explained in detail later. But on the larger issue of representation, there are a number of points that should be mentioned.
It is clear to the committee that this bill is different from any other one in that we have altered, since the last redistribution in 1947, the basis of calculating the membership of the house from the several provinces. Section 2 of the bill carries out the changes which we have made. There have, of course, been increases and decreases in the several provinces. For example, the province of Ontario gains two seats according to the last census. The province of Quebec gains two seats. The province of British Columbia gains four seats. For other reasons the district of Mackenzie has been granted an additional seat. There have been decreases, in Nova Scotia of one seat, in Manitoba of two seats, and in Saskatchewan of three seats.
As a result of the committee work, there have been a great many changes in the constituency boundaries. For the sake of the record it should be pointed out that in the province of Newfoundland there has been only one change and that six constituencies have been left the same. In the province of Nova Scotia there are five changes and seven constituencies are the same, all the changes being brought about by the necessity for the loss of one seat. The province of New Brunswick has been left as it was before, with ten seats the same. The same applies with respect to the province of Prince Edward Island with four seats. In the province of Quebec there are two new seats, 45 are the same and 28 changes have been made. May I add that most of the changes or a considerable number of them have been descriptive
Redistribution
changes. Might I also add that I understand from the committee that all the changes have met with unanimous approval of all the members of the provincial subcommittee.
In Ontario there are two new seats, 49 are the same and 34 have changes. In Manitoba and Saskatchewan there have been changes in all the seats because of the reduction in numbers in those two provinces. In Alberta two are the same and there have been 15 changes. It might be noted that last time there were no changes in Alberta. In British Columbia there are four seats added, seven are the same and there are 11 changes. The result is that in the provinces there are eight new seats, 130 are the same as heretofore and 125 have been changed.
On Saturday there was considerable discussion about improving the method of doing this work. I have no desire to make any remarks with regard to that debate, except to say this. In my opinion the members of the committee have found themselves seized with knowledge of the conditions not only in their own constituencies but in others and have contributed materially to the discussions in the committee and to the decisions which have been made as reflected in the schedule.
I want to add my thanks to those which have already been expressed for the work of that committee.
As to the procedure to be adopted with respect to this bill, I should point out that in 1947 a general discussion was permitted on section 1. In fact, on that occasion amendments to the schedule were moved on section 1 of the bill, and the government of the day took some objection to that course. At any rate, it was suggested that it might be better if the discussion on the schedules took place on the schedules. I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that in conformity with the suggestion made in 1947, we should discuss the sections of the bill on their merits, leaving section 3 to stand, as it relates directly to the schedules. Then, as we come to the schedules, have a general discussion on the first item of each province with respect to the whole of that province. If that does not meet with the wishes of the committee, I would point out that there are a number of amendments to be moved to some of the schedules, and that it would be desirable to have those amendments before the committee so that the discussion which would take place then on section 1 might have in mind the changes in the schedules.
May I also add this. Hon. members may have before them two copies of the bill and the schedule. One was printed on Saturday in the desire to get this information before the members at the earliest possible moment.

Redistribution
There were a number of errors in the printing, and in fact a number of errors in the interpretation of what the committee has decided. Most of those-all for all I know- have been corrected in a reprinted bill which is now before the hon. members. Nevertheless, there are some changes yet to be made, and if hon. members have a purely descriptive change to suggest I would be glad to receive it so that we can check it with the original. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we proceed with the bill section by section, without a discussion of the schedules, leaving section 3 to stand. Then, permit a general discussion on the first item of each provincial schedule with respect to that province. If, Mr. Chairman, you feel that that is not the proper procedure, then I would ask leave to move a number of amendments before we have a discussion on section 1.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
In so far as the suggestion that we proceed section by section without engaging in a general debate on section 1 is concerned, I would point out the reasons why that is not practical for the purpose of dealing with the matters that are concerning many hon. members at this time.
The well-accepted practice in this house in the committee stage has been to regard the first section as the point at which general discussion can take place. The general discussion will be largely guided by the result of the decisions that are made outside of this house which find themselves interpreted in the schedule to the bill. The minister has already indicated that he proposes to move a number of amendments to the schedule, and that indicates reasons why hon. members are not yet in a position to discuss the general effect of this bill as it stands with full knowledge of what the situation really is.
There is no reason to repeat any of the arguments that have been made as to the desirability or undesirability of this system. It would be improper if I sought to repeat any arguments as to the desirability of appointing a commission to deal with this. The house has made its decision. I simply make that observation so that no one will think that we are accepting this as a desirable system. We simply accept the decision that has been made by a majority of this house that we are to proceed in this way, and by the decisions of a committee of this kind. Therefore, by the rules of the house, we are compelled to make the best we can of a bad job. Let no one be in any doubt that it is a bad job. The task, however, should be to try to achieve the best results that can be achieved under an unsatisfactory system.

The minister has himself pointed out that the discussion can best take place with knowledge of what the schedule contains. I am simply stating what is known to all members of this house, or I imagine is known to all, when I say that there is still discussion taking place in regard to some of the constituencies. That being so, we are still not certain as to what the recommendation is to be in regard to certain of the constituencies covered by this schedule which is before us in printed form.
The minister has indicated that he will move certain amendments if we are to proceed with a general discussion at this time on section 1. The minister is of course aware that at this very moment discussion is taking place in regard to further changes in boundaries, I think it would be best that we wait until we know that any amendments that are to be made by the minister, who has been the chairman of the general committee, are in fact ready to be presented so that we are not dealing with a varying schedule, but with a schedule that is to be before us as the basis of discussion.
There are a number of other items of business that we can proceed with in the meantime. I think that to avoid any discussion that may be unnecessary we should not carry forward the general debate, or the debate in regard to any of the sections which affect the schedule, until we know what the schedule really is that we are discussing. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, simply to facilitate the procedure and to avoid debate that may perhaps become strenuous, as it has on other occasions in the past, when subjects of this kind were under discussion, I propose that we will save time by postponing discussion on this bill until the decisions have been reached and the minister is in a position to say: This is the complete schedule that is being proposed by the committee of the house.
We already know from one or two of the exchanges that took place on Saturday that strong opinions will be expressed in regard to particular constituencies. It is conceivable that some changes that are still to be made may have some bearing on the extent of the debate. I therefore, Mr. Chairman, with the thought in mind simply of avoiding unnecessary debate and with the knowledge that we have a great deal of business to proceed with otherwise, move that the committee rise to report later this day at the call of the chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

section 3 be not called, but that the bill be proceeded with in other respects.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

I wonder if I might make a suggestion. Perhaps it is in the form of a compromise, but in dealing with redistribution there are lots of compromises. I believe the leader of the opposition is perfectly justified in asking that the debate on clause 1, which is as general a debate as we can have in committee, should not be proceeded with until we have a more complete picture as to what is to be in the schedule. Therefore, I support him in the suggestion that the debate on clause 1 should be deferred.
I wonder, however, whether it is necessary to postpone all of the discussion to a later time. The leader of the opposition has said that there are constituencies in some provinces which are still under discussion at various levels. Some of the provinces are agreed to. In some other cases, although the decisions arrived at are those of the majority and may not be satisfactory to some of the rest of us, at least we know that there are no further discussions taking place. As a compromise I wonder whether we could not let all the sections of the bill stand and proceed with the schedule, taking up the provinces on which there has been agreement or in connection with which there are no further discussions outside of the house. In that way we can get part of the work done without forgoing the right for which the leader of the opposition has asked, and which I support, to have general discussion after we have the whole schedule before us. As I say, I make this suggestion as a compromise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hon. members realize that the motion of the leader of the opposition is not debatable, and it is my duty to put it forthwith. If it is the sense of the committee-and with the approval of the leader of the opposition-that some compromise suggestion be made before I put the motion, it is quite agreeable to me. But my duty is to put the motion immediately.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to bend the rule in any way in regard to debates, but perhaps it would simplify matters if I indicated why I would not wish to concur in the suggestion made. I point out that, so long as it is understood that changes may be made, I do not know how any of us is to be sure that there might not be some change made which would greatly affect the general discussion in regard to this subject, or even the discussion in regard to a particular province, although we might think at the moment that the schedule is complete in regard to that province. For that reason I would ask that the vote be taken on the motion I have made.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot debate over again the merits of an argument that has been made and disposed of. But I have made and indicated our desire to facilitate the discussion, with the information before us as the basis of that discussion. I suggest that it is not a proper procedure to deal with a schedule until the section indicating the existence of the schedule has been adopted. One need not extend the argument to disclose what an extraordinary result there would be if one could defer the discussion of a section of an act, and then engage in a discussion of a schedule which, at least in theory, might never be adopted, or might never become a reality until the section giving it validity is approved.
The other point I would make is that in an important matter of this kind the whole effect of the act is not related merely to the satisfaction of individual members from any province, but it is related to the belief on

the part of the hon. members and the House of Commons generally that what we are doing is in the best interests of Canada as a whole.
We do not think this is the best system, but we must accept it. Having been called upon to accept it, by a majority vote, it is our duty to do the best we can to make sure that we discuss this matter with knowledge of the way this method is going to work. That is governed largely by knowledge of what is happening, not in any single province but rather in different provinces.
It may well be that there is some single province where at least no very vigorous dissatisfaction will be expressed as a result of the sins of commission, no matter how strong the views may be in regard to the sins of omission. That does not become a subject for discussion by members representing only a particular province; it is a subject for discussion and concern on the part of all members. In my opinion we cannot proceed by the method indicated unless there is consent, and I do not think I should give that consent as I believe the business of the house will be expedited by proceeding with other business.

They could then decide what they wished to do with regard to the schedule because at that moment the minister would be in a position to move the amendments of which he has given notice.
If that suggestion is agreeable it seems to me that it would permit the committee to make some progress toward the adoption of sections 2 and 4 to 11 inclusive. Mr. Chairman, section 1 of the bill now provides an opportunity to discuss the procedure that has taken place. We are bound to do the best we can under the method that has been adopted. There may have been some who thought that the vigorous terms applied to a procedure of this kind by the hon. member for Quebec South would not be justified on this occasion because there had been assurances that the government would seek the co-operation and support of all hon. members. There might have been a number of hon. members who placed a great deal of hope in those assurances, but the fact remains that no matter how sincerely those assurances may have been given on behalf of the government, the actual procedure has not conformed with them in any way. It is true that attempts have been made to make certain concessions in regard to specific objections which have been brought before the different provincial committees, nevertheless the net result is that we find that there have been acts of barefaced gerrymandering never exceeded under the committee system or under any other system since confederation.
One of the difficulties in discussing this point with complete certainty as to the full extent of what is to be done at the present time is that further proposals are under consideration right now outside of the house which may to some extent modify the criticism that can be directed against the decisions as to certain particular constituencies. Even the changes now under consideration, however, will not remove the criticism as to the results of the procedure that has been followed. It may be that the full extent of what was contemplated with respect to the electoral district of Lake Centre may be modified, as I most earnestly hope it will, but that does not get away from what was originally contemplated. As a result of the most vigorous expression of opinion outside of the house I would hope that members of the committee dealing with the problem of redistribution have been impressed with the desirability of reconsideration of the proposals that they will put forward in final form with respect to

Redistribution
that particular constituency. It is significant, however, that the changes that have been made have so conspicuously been efforts to affect those constituencies represented by Conservative members in the house.

speechtext: And Liberal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

That of course may be described as simply an accident of geography or an accident of the movement of population. It is very interesting that such sweeping changes were proposed with respect to the constituency of Lake Centre which is represented by a member who is recognized as one of the outstanding members of the Conservative party. I would point out that this practice has been carried out in other cases. In Manitoba it is significant that there is to be a gerrymander there by the joining of the Souris and Brandon ridings. I find it difficult to believe that most members will agree that the only adjustment of boundaries that could have taken place was one which would join a riding, which for so many years had been represented by the very distinguished member of parliament from Souris, with a riding which was won in a by-election by one of the younger but distinguished members of this party last year.
That kind of union of constituencies is of the type that led to the original adoption of the word "gerrymander". I feel sure all hon. members of the house know the source of the word. It perpetuates the name of a senator in the United States who found it convenient to propose a union of electoral areas which would do away with the riding of one of his opponents. On that occasion the boundaries suggested had such a strange outline that one of those present at the meeting of that particular committee, held as long ago as 1812, said that it looked like a salamander, which is a particularly unpleasant looking type of reptile. Another said it should no longer be regarded as a salamander but as a gerrymander. From that time this unusual and rather ugly word-

I have indicated already that I am not placing before the house any suggestion that either party comes into the house cloaked in robes of virtue so far as the question of redistribution is concerned. We had hoped however that, with the assurance that was given and with the very strong statements that have been

The number of people he will be called upon to serve will be approximately 50 per cent more than the two adjoining constituencies which were under consideration in the same deliberations. Perhaps it will be said that there is no significance in the fact that these two other constituencies are represented by Liberal members, and that it is entirely one of the accidents of geography that the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings will find himself called upon to serve that larger number of people. I feel sure he will be happy to serve them with the same efficiency and effectiveness with which he has served his present constituency in the past. Nevertheless he is called upon to represent a much larger number of people than in the constituencies nearby, and that hardly conforms with the general principle of representation by population which was supposed to be the basis of the redistribution that we are undertaking.
One of the difficulties with which we are confronted in matters of this kind is that, proceeding as we do under an unsatisfactory system with no basic policy adopted as to how the redistribution will be carried out, there is nothing that can be done but an utterly unmodified form of log-rolling in an effort to ameliorate the injuries that result from this kind of political gerrymandering. Another difficulty with which we are confronted is that in these matters the Liberal party speaks with two voices. They are both clear and unmistakable voices. One is the voice of virtue and of memory. The other is the voice of political expediency. When the subject is being discussed on a theoretical basis then from memory and experience members of the Liberal party speak in a way that all of us can support. We have already heard the statements of the hon. member for Quebec South read into the record, and many of us have heard

him make these statements in the house. Statements of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King have been read into the record, statements he made both when he was prime minister and when he was leader of the opposition. A great number of statements can be cited here as to the high purpose of those seeking redistribution.
Another example of that kind of statement in regard to the desirability of an altruistic approach to this subject was contained in the words of the Hon. Colin Gibson at the time redistribution was under consideration a few years ago. At that time he was Secretary of State, and speaking of the hopes in regard to the committee he had this to say:
I may say again referring to past history, that since the new method has been, adopted of referring the question of delineating the constituencies to a special committee of the house, agreement has recently been arrived at owing to the fact that a real effort was made by all members of the committee to be fair, just and reasonable. I have every confidence the same spirit of justice and fair play will be displayed by those who form the committee this year.
That was the high and lofty statement made in regard to the actions of a committee which were described later by the member for Quebec South as the application of the law of the jungle. One was the voice of memory, the voice of altruism, and the other was the voice of reality indicating exactly what had happened in the meetings of the committee and in this house.
I am compelled, Mr. Chairman, to remember other words of the hon. member for Quebec South, because he has spoken with a frankness which still indicates reasons why we might have hoped for more from this committee. Writing in an article which has been referred to from time to time, and which appeared in Maclean's magazine, the hon. member for Quebec South spoke of his regret that the Liberal party needed to be saved from opportunism which neglected principle, and which is begotten of what can only be called the office-holding mania. Those are not my words, but the words of the hon. member for Quebec South who has spoken with that measure of frankness which we might have hoped would have, in some measure, guided the course of the committee dealing with this subject at this time.
Although my motion that the committee should rise has been turned down, I would point out that it is in order for the minister who is guiding this measure through the house to move at any time that the committee rise and report progress. I repeat the suggestion, with the further discussion we have had, that he follow this course. I have suggested reasons why this should be done. I

would point out that I have only mentioned a few of the examples of what has happened in the province of Ontario. There are very serious examples of gerrymandering which affect the hon. member for Huron; which affect the hon. member for Frontenac, where that historic constituency is being merged completely with another constituency; which affect ridings right across the province of Ontario. These examples can be discussed in detail if the further arguments that are presented fail to convince the minister of the desirability of reconsidering this subject.
It is true, Mr. Chairman, that under the procedure now before us it will not be possible to carry out redistribution in a manner which can give the people of Canada very much confidence in what is being done to assure some measure of representation by population. Nevertheless, some of the most glaring examples of gerrymandering, of the law of the jungle to use the term employed by the hon. member for Quebec South, could be avoided if this committee would rise and refer these most glaring cases back to the redistribution committee to be considered while the house is proceeding with other important business, which could be dealt with satisfactorily in the meantime.

Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, it is still in order for us to recite some of the experiences we have had in the committee, and to register our objection to the method still being employed, namely that of having redistribution effected by a committee of the House of Commons. What happened this time is practically the same as what happened in 1947, a time when many of us who were members of this committee were also members of that committee, and I have reason to believe it is similar to the experience of former committees.
A special committee of the House of Commons was appointed. That committee, Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS

The subcommittee met; some of them shortly after they were established, but some of them did not meet for quite a long time. In every case with which I had any connection I think it is correct to report that, although our official subcommittee met and took the formal decisions, whether they were unanimous or by a majority, the real decisions were not made in the subcommittees. The hon. member for Ottawa West can speak for Ontario but as to some of the other provinces, particularly my own, there is no question but that there were meetings of the Liberal caucus for the province as a whole. What happened was that, in the case of Manitoba, the first meeting we had was one with nothing laid before us. The chairman invited us all to make suggestions. It was a surprise and a most welcome one. We made suggestions. Then the next time we met a map was presented to us. By some strange coincidence, that map appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press in Winnipeg on the same afternoon that we obtained it here. That was on May 23.
From that day on we really went to work and our method of proceeding was that we on the subcommittee would make protests, counter-suggestions and proposals and the Liberal members of the committee would take our proposals back to the Liberal caucus. We give them full credit for doing that and for doing it repeatedly. I have lost track of the number of times that our proposals were taken back to the Liberal caucus in order to ascertain whether or not they would approve of the suggestions that were made. In giving credit, let me go further and say that some of our suggestions were accepted. Indeed the final map is quite different from the one published on May 23, and it is an improvement. But even if the Liberals had accepted all of our proposals-and they certainly did not-what I object to is the method of procedure. The real decisions were made not by the subcommittee which had its official status but by the Liberal caucus. That was the course followed in the case of Manitoba, to my knowledge; and I imagine that it was followed with regard to a number of other provinces as well.
Even if the results of that procedure were perfectly fair having regard to the members affected, and even though the map had the appearance of being a proper one, I suggest that the procedure lends itself to serious criticism and people wonder whether that is the right way to do it. As a matter of fact as a result of that procedure you do not get a perfectly fair map; and when there are any unfairnesses, the people of the country are led to the conclusion that redistribution is being done on a political basis.
One of the other factors involved in this method is-

I know that it would now be out of order for me to talk about an independent commission, so I am not repeating those arguments at this time. I am simply reporting to you, Mr. Chairman, on what actually happened in the work of the committee which produced the report and which produced the schedule that is now before us.
The other point I wish to emphasize is that in our committee discussions, inevitably- it is inherent in the nature of the system- we have concerned ourselves with present boundaries and whether or not they should be adjusted, and we have concerned ourselves with sitting members. I want to make it perfectly clear that I am not speaking in any holier-than-thou attitude. No member of the House of Commons who has been a member of that committee has been able to divorce himself from the necessity of considering present boundaries, the situations of which he is aware in his own province, and the situations with respect to particular members. It is precisely because it is inherent in the nature of the system that we take such considerations into account that I deplore the fact that we have been doing it in that way on this occasion. It seems to me that what we should be concerned with is not the situation of particular members, not the question of whether or not a boundary is an historic one, but rather with the right of the people of the country to proper voice in parliament as nearly on a representation by population basis as it is possible for us to achieve.
In my view in some parts of the country some progress has been made towards that objective. There are many cases in which glaring inequalities have been lessened. There has been some improvement. In fact, in some of the provinces I will say that the only things that are wrong are actual omissions; what has been done has been good, but that the committee has not gone far enough because it is inevitably hamstrung by the very conditions under which it has had to work.
Having made those general observations with respect to the work of the committee, may I say that I utter those comments not in order to cast any reflection on the individuals who have been engaged in this work. There have been many attempts to be fair. There has been a good deal of considering and reconsidering of proposals made by opposition members. In fact, that consideration is still going on at the present time. I ask that no members take offence at the suggestion that the work in which they have been involved is work they should not have

been doing at all. It is not they, who are at fault; it is the system. The result is that we now have before us a schedule in which there remain many unfairnesses and as a result there will be in the country the feeling that they arise from political considerations.
May I now make a few comments with respect to what has been done in my own province of Manitoba. We have been under the necessity of losing two seats. That fact creates a problem which our friends in Ontario do not know much about. If they have difficulties when they get two new seats, I wonder what their experience would be if they had to lose seats in proportion to the number we have had to lose. The two which have been taken out by the decision of the majority of the committee are the constituency of Souris and the constituency of Selkirk.
It is true that two constituencies have to come out. But in the subcommittee we offered suggestions alternative to those that were made. I will not spend any time on the alternative suggestions with regard to Souris because I have no doubt that the hon. member for Souris, who is a member of the committee, will have something to say about them. However, I want to register my strong objection to the elimination of the present riding of Selkirk. On the map of Manitoba there is to be retained a riding to be called Selkirk but it is really the present riding of Norquay, with the town of Selkirk added to it, with the name of Selkirk to be applied to that riding. The present riding of Selkirk is a suburban riding. It includes St. James, West Kildonan and adjoining territory and the town of Selkirk. This riding is to be eliminated. I object to that elimination. I naturally object to it because of the person involved, namely my own close personal friend, the hon. member for Selkirk. Many other members of the house will be unhappy about that change because many hon. members regard him as a close personal friend, as a splendid member of this house-

-and one who some of us are confident will be back again. But I make my protest against the elimination of that seat not on those personal grounds. I make it on two other grounds. The first one I can state briefly. It is this. Selkirk was one of the largest of the non-Winnipeg ridings in the province of Manitoba. One might understand the argument for eliminating Souris-even if my friend the hon. member for Souris does not like it-on the basis that it was the smallest riding in the province in terms of population. Yes; very much the largest of all those ridings. In addition to that objection which I have registered to the elimination of the present Selkirk, I also register most strongly my objection to the increasing disparity which we are called upon to take in the province of Manitoba as between the population in distinctly rural seats and that in distinctly urban seats. It is fully recognized that distinctly rural seats are entitled to a slightly less population unit than distinctly urban seats. I not only recognize that principle, I assert it. There is no question about it. But it seems to me that we have allowed abuse of that principle to be carried too far in some areas in this country. I am glad to see in the province of Ontario that it is being reversed a little bit, if not sufficiently; but in the province of Manitoba a disparity which was already too great has been made even greater. And in my view the urban people in the province of Manitoba are being grossly discriminated against in the matter of proper and adequate representation in the House of Commons.
I want to demonstrate that, Mr. Chairman, with a few figures, and I will naturally keep my figures to a minimum. I want to tell the committee what the situation was as a result of the last redistribution, and then show the committee what has happened as a result of this redistribution, which indicates a trend against the rights of the urban people of the Winnipeg area.
As a result of the last redistribution, which was based on the 1941 census, we ended up with sixteen seats in the province of Manitoba. Three of these seats were combined urban and rural areas. They were Brandon, St. Boniface and Selkirk. Their total population was 125,176, or an average of 41,725. I have put that on the record, but I shall omit any reference to these three seats from the argument I shall make in a moment because they are urban-rural seats and cannot be included in any comparison between distinctly urban and distinctly rural constituencies. Having put that information with respect to these three seats off by itself, the rest of the picture was in these terms. There were left nine rural seats, distinctly rural, whose total population was 365,683, making an average population per distinctly rural seat of 40,631.
	'
I move on to the urban situation as a result of the last redistribution. There were four distinctly urban seats, Winnipeg North, Winnipeg North Centre, Winnipeg South, Winnipeg South Centre. Their total population was 238,885, or an average of 59,721.
I have given you the average population in the distinctly rural seats and the average population in the distinctly urban seats following the last redistribution, Mr. Chairman. The difference between these two averages, between 40,631 for the rural and 59,721 for the urban, was 19,090. I ask hon. members to note that that figure of 19,090 was the spread between the average rural and the average urban seat following the last redistribution. I ask them also to note that on that basis the average urban seat had 46 per cent more population than the average rural seat. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that that disparity of 46 per cent, which was the result of the last redistribution, was unfair. It was too great. It was a case of discrimination against the rights of the people of the Winnipeg area on any theory of representation by population.
In the bill which is still on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Quebec South a number of rules are suggested. I make it clear that those rules are not yet the law of this land, but they do reflect the thinking of one hon. member who has given considerable attention to this whole question. The hon. member for Winnipeg South suggests in his bill that an urban seat should be one and a quarter times the size of rural seats in population. His suggestion therefore is that the disparity should be 25 per cent. We were handed in the last redistribution in Manitoba a disparity of 46 per cent.

Now let us come down to the results of this redistribution, bearing in mind that the last one gave us a disparity of 46 per cent, which I regarded as too high. On this occasion we are left with only two of these combined or rural-urban seats, namely, Brandon-Souris and St. Boniface, with a total

population of 107,002, or an average of 53,501. As to distinctly rural seats, we are left with eight, and their total population is 351,704, or an average per rural seat of 43,963. As against that, Mr. Chairman, we now have four distinctly urban seats, whose population make a total of 307,782 or an average of 76,945 per urban seat. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, whereas before we had a disparity of 19,090 or 46 per cent, that disparity is now 32,982 or 75 per cent. To put it in other words, 351,704 rural persons are given eight seats; almost the same number of urban persons, 307,782, will have only four seats. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is going too far.
I congratulate the Ontario committee on having moved a bit in the other direction. I do not think they moved far enough, but they moved in the right direction. In Manitoba we have moved in the wrong direction. We had a disparity against the city of 46 per cent. It should be only 25 per cent, says the hon. member for Quebec South, and that disparity is now being increased to 75 per cent.
There is room in some parts of the country for perhaps more disparity than the hon. member for Quebec South has suggested, but I suggest that in a province like Manitoba, where we have quite a few fairly populous centres out through the rural areas-Portage la Prairie calls itself a city, and there are other points through the province which are quite populous and increasingly so-there is no excuse for that disparity of 75 per cent. Perhaps it is not appropriate for me to discuss it here, but I may say that back home in Manitoba at the provincial level we have the same kind of unfair disparity between the urban and the rural areas and I would suggest-

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Is it the policy of the C.C.F. party that urban constituencies should have the same population as the rural constituencies?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I thought I made it perfectly clear that I accept the idea that the population in the rural constituencies should be less than the population in the urban constituencies. I went further and agreed with the proposal made by the hon. member for Quebec South that the difference should be of the order of 25 per cent. What I am objecting to is the difference of 75 per cent that is proposed by the redistribution that is now placed before us, which surely no one can defend. I know that in some quarters this is regarded as a touchy subject, and that one should not speak about it, but surely fairness should underlie our redistribution. Surely we
Redistribution
do not throw the idea of representation by population completely out the window, and I contend that this is a grossly unfair redistribution so far as the city of Winnipeg is concerned.
In reply to the hon. member for Norquay, may I tell him that when one makes a complaint such as I have made-and I made it in the committee on redistribution-he has an obligation to suggest an alternative, and I did suggest an alternative. My alternative proposal was that there should have been retained in the Winnipeg area a fifth seat, one something like the present Selkirk, consisting of a suburban area around the city of Winnipeg, together with some of the country area just outside of that suburban part. If one did that he could create three urban-rural seats-I mean, in the province- three including the additional one in the Winnipeg area which I suggested-with an average population of 53,487. That would leave four distinctly urban seats inside the city limits with an average population of 66,080, and seven distinctly rural seats with an average population of 48,814. That would thus add an extra seat to the Winnipeg area and it would lessen the grossly unfair disparity in the map proposed by the committee in its majority report.
That is my answer to the hon. member, not only in general but in specific terms. The proposal which I made in committee- and I still have in my hand the typewritten figures I then used-suggested a disparity of 33 per cent. My proposal was that the distinctly rural seats should have 48,814, that the distinctly urban seats should have 66,080, which would have made each rural seat 17,660 less than each urban seat, or would represent a difference of 33 per cent.
In other words, in the light of the situation in Manitoba I was prepared to go even further than the hon. member for Quebec South, who suggested a disparity of 25 per cent, for I proposed a disparity of 33 per cent. But I certainly suggest that a disparity of 46 per cent such as we were handed last time was too great, and that a disparity of 75 per cent, which we are being handed now, is scandalous. It offends against the principle of representation by population, even with all the qualifications and modifications of that principle that are sometimes put forward, and simply cannot be defended.
One realizes that at this stage of the game amendments do not get anywhere, and that there is no point in moving any further changes at this time in the Manitoba situation; but I do protest strongly and I do insist that there should have been retained another suburban seat around Winnipeg, such as the

Redistribution
present seat of Selkirk, and that it should have been done so as to retain a closer resemblance to the principle of representation by population than is involved in the redistribution now before us.
I wish to make it very clear that if the population in Manitoba stays on the basis which now obtains, or if it moves still further in the direction of a greater concentration in the urban area, as has been the case during the last ten years, then when the next redistribution, comes around we simply must not have this kind of map for Manitoba. We must have for the city of Winnipeg and for the greater Winnipeg area a number of seats more in proportion to that to which we are entitled, which will call at least for five seats where we now have only four. I would settle for a 25 per cent disparity-I would even settle for 33 per cent-but none of this 46 per cent and 75 per cent, which means that in Manitoba every four Canadians out in the country has the same voice in the House of Commons as have every seven Canadians living in the Winnipeg area. And when you multiply that disparity by similar disparities, or others even approaching it in other provinces-although I believe the worst disparity may be in Manitoba-you get a completely unfair balance in the House of Commons, so far as representation of the people of this country is concerned.
This, again, is another of the reasons why we feel it is wrong that this matter has been dealt with in a parliamentary committee. This is the sort of thing which could be corrected if it were dealt with by some outside body, under rules given to it by the house, a body having the right and the authority to go ahead and to apply those rules objectively and fairly, and in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole, instead of only with an eye to what obtains at the present time.
Then, just one further word about Manitoba. It will be argued in defence of the map proposed that there is equality within the categories. That is true. Within the category of rural seats they are all in the forty thousands, varying from 40,000 to 47,000-and I commend that to some other provinces. Within the category of urban-rural seats, they are both in the fifty thousands. Within the category of urban seats, three of them are 75,000, and one is 80,000-so that they are close together.
But I submit that the virtue of equality within those categories does not get away from the fact that there is too great a disparity between the categories, in particular between the average for urban seats and the average for rural seats. It is the violation of that principle which has resulted in the loss

of the seat of my hon. friend from Selkirk- a result which we think is most unfair. The violation of that principle is something which one just cannot accept as being fair to the people of the greater Winnipeg area, and indeed to the other urban centres in Manitoba. If we cannot have it corrected this time, then I hope when the next redistribution comes along we will have something more akin to fairness and more akin to the rules suggested by the hon. member for Quebec South.

Mr. Chairman, I would not want this discussion to be concluded without saying a word about the redistribution in Manitoba. I feel impelled to do so, not only because of the interest I have personally, and which my constituents in the city of Winnipeg have, but also because of the attitude taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has preceded me in the debate.
It is not to be interpreted that, representing as I have for a long time part of the city of Winnipeg, I am not most desirous that those people who now elect four members from greater Winnipeg should be entitled to every consideration possible in the matter of representation in the House of Commons. I am on record during an earlier discussion in this session as having said that the principle of representation by population has been given very wide lip service in this country, but that its application has not been attempted across the country as a whole. Even within the provinces there have been wide discrepancies.
I join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in rejoicing in the fact that in Ontario some approach has been made to drawing closer together the figures of representation between rural and urban constituencies. But I would point out to him and to the committee, and to any others who may be interested, that the situation in Ontario is hardly parallel with that in Manitoba, because there are comparatively few rural areas in Ontario which do not have urban centres in the form of large towns or smaller cities, most of which are larger than anything we have in Manitoba outside Winnipeg, with the possible exception of the city of Brandon.

This time, however, although I was not on the committee, it has been a matter of satisfaction to realize that we have come much closer to equality of representation within the urban areas themselves. The hon. member has pointed out that there is a spread of less than 5,000 among the four constituencies, and that three of them are within a thousand. He has also pointed out that, with the narrowness of the spread in the strictly rural areas, we have an approximation of equality in population between those two ridings which include the major cities in our province, and a fairly large rural area, namely Brandon and St. Boniface.
Right away I will say I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he says that in another five or ten years we will have to pay more attention to the redistribution of representation within the province, weighting the strictly urban areas more heavily. That principle has been acknowledged already in the last redistribution in Manitoba, although there the city of Winnipeg is represented only by slightly less than one-fifth membership in the legislature whereas even under this new arrangement we have about 30 per cent of the federal representation.
I think it is only fair to point out that when we had the federal redistribution five years ago Manitoba lost a seat. We sacrificed one of the rural ridings in that redistribution; the city of Winnipeg was not called upon to make any sacrifice. We are now to lose two seats, one of which is Souris which is a strictly rural constituency. It has no large-sized urban centre, being made up of smaller towns and villages.
We have had to bear in mind throughout the years that while the province is becoming industrialized to a large extent, while there has been a tendency to concentrate population in the urban areas, there is a perfectly sound reason for weighting rather more heavily the urban centres in arriving at the representation. I say that although I represent a city riding.

The hon. member spoke rather sadly about the elimination in this redistribution of the present constituency of Selkirk and expressed his personal regard for the sitting member. Apart from politics I share that regard, as I am sure do all hon. members of the house. However, we must look at the logic of what has happened. We must remember that the constituency of Selkirk was created for the first time five years ago. It does not have either the geographical homogeneity or the tradition which applies to many other constituencies. I was not on the committee, but I knew what was happening, and it seems perfectly natural to me that with the readjustment which was necessary the proper procedure to follow was the one which has been followed.
Another step has been taken which I am sure will commend itself to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, namely, that we have drawn back into an urban area where there is a community of interest-this is important in matters of representation-both St. James and the Kildonans. While this has served to enlarge the seats of the Winnipeg members, except my own-mine is increased only to a small extent-I think it was a just redistribution and lays the foundation, if I may put it that way, for the point of view which the hon. gentleman has expressed as being desirable.
In my opinion we have not reached a state in the development of Manitoba where we are able to express adequately within the areas which the hon. gentleman and I and others represent, the general opinion of the province of Manitoba from the purely urban standpoint. While I regret, as I think everyone must regret, the increasing disparity between urban and rural ridings, we have made a substantial step toward the equalization of representation in each of these areas and we have approached full parity in the other two constituencies of Brandon and St. Boniface.
I do not know what the experience of my hon. friend has been, nor do 1 know what the experience of other hon. members who represent Winnipeg ridings has been, but I

have had no sustained or substantial protests against the increased disparity. Perhaps we in Manitoba have become accustomed-

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by commenting on the fact that this important matter comes before us at this late stage of the session. The bill is before us now because the committee continued to sit up until Saturday night. A great deal of work was done during that period and indeed over the week end by the secretary of the committee and others who had duties in connection with the preparation of the boundaries in the schedule to the bill. I think it is only proper that we should make a sincere acknowledgment of the efforts and extraordinary exertions made by the staff of the house, particularly the clerk of the committee, Mr. Chasse, in having the schedule prepared in its present form.
I think it is regrettable that the work has had to be done under such pressure. Even with the real and desperate efforts that have been made during the last day or two in proof-reading and checking the boundaries of constituencies, I am quite satisfied that even after the bill has had extended consideration, there will still be errors in it. I do not think a work as important as this should have to be done under such pressure and in such haste. It would have been much better had some of the alternative suggestions been accepted; it would have been much better had this bill been allowed to stand over for further consideration to a later stage of this session in November.
The chairman of the committee, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in summing up the recommendations of the committee in general terms said that in the provinces it is proposed to create eight new constituencies; it is proposed that 125 constituencies be changed and that 130 remain unchanged. In speaking on second reading of the bill on Saturday I drew attention to the fact that as

long as the present method of dealing with redistribution by a partisan committee is followed-when I say "partisan" I mean a committee composed of partisans from aU parts of the house; it nevertheless still is a partisan committee with a majority of the partisans representing the party which holds the majority of the seats in the house-it is impossible to expect that principle will be followed or that it will be followed consistently. The fruits of such a system are to be seen in the glaring inequalities that appear before us, the strange and wonderful abortions of sizes and shapes of boundaries, and the complete disregard in so many cases of anything resembling a consistent retention of and adherence to principle.
In passing let me give one or two illustrations. According to the report of the committee the riding in Canada which will have the lowest population will have, under the 1951 census figures, a population of 9,999. While I have not the exact figures, the constituency with the largest population will have a population of some 91,000. Making all proper allowance, for we all do make allowance, for the necessity for giving larger and weighted representation to rural constituencies compared with urban, I say there are discrepancies here that simply cannot stand up to examination in the light of principle. Let us take the province of Ontario. We faced the fact that on the new basis the average population for the constituencies would be 54,000, and really desperate efforts were made to boost over the 30,000 mark all constituencies that had been below 30,000 in population. But we have finished up in Ontario, in the light of the schedule, plus the amendments proposed this morning by the chairman of the Ontario subcommittee, the hon. member for Ottawa West, with results like these. The constituency with the lowest population will continue to have about 28,000 and the constituency with the highest population will have about 91,000.
Making all proper allowances for what I have said is recognized by all parties and all members of the house, the necessity for taking account of the size of constituencies and the necessity for giving weighted representation to rural compared with urban ridings, we now face a situation such as I have described, and I say you simply cannot justify it in the light of any serious attempt to apply principles consistently.
Under this method we also see a defensive attitude taken by all members of the committee. I do not draw any distinction between parties in this respect because it is only to be expected that as long as we are working under the committee method a defensive attitude is going to be taken by

most when it comes to tampering with or changing ridings in which fellow partisans are the sitting members. I also wish to say, and I sought to emphasize this on Saturday, that after the experience I have had in sitting on the committee I am not unaware of the difficulties faced by those who represented the majority party on the committee. I am quite aware that they have had their difficulties too as well as those of us who represented opposition parties on the committee.
The hon. member for Ottawa West said this morning that there were no meetings of the Ontario caucus of the Liberal party from the time the committee began its work until the present time. The hon. member has made his statement. Nevertheless we were told on numbers of occasions that their members would not accept some quite reasonable and proper suggestions that we put before the committee. We were told: Our caucus for such and such a part of the province will not accept that. I leave it at that.

As has already been indicated, the bulk of the work is done in the subcommittees. That is only natural because that is the proper starting point, but I have a very serious criticism to make of the way the main committee worked. It may be, like so many of the criticisms one has had to make, that it is something inherent in the present system, but the fact of the matter is that the main committee, when dealing with the reports of the various provincial subcommittees, gave very brief consideration to them. Attempts were made by opposition members to explain in a general way, but as far as members from other provinces were concerned-I am speaking now of the government members on the committee as I tried to observe them-I do not think there was very much attempt made to understand the problems of other provinces or the reports of the subcommittees from other provinces than that of the individual government member concerned.
It would be very interesting today to call upon members of the main committee to sit down and write an examination testing their knowledge of the recommendations of the committee respecting changes in boundaries in other provinces than the one in which they happen to reside. I think such a test would produce some interesting results. I mentioned on Saturday that when at one time I said in the Ontario subcommittee that I would carry a particular matter to the main committee I was met with the answer: "You will not change anything in the main committee." That was an answer by one of the
Redistribution
government supporters in the committee- "you will not change anything in the main committee." How perfectly true that was, Mr. Chairman! It was just a case of going through a matter of form in the main committee. A subcommittee from one province would make its report and the government members from the other provinces were there to stand up and vote. Nothing was changed in the main committee. I am saying critically that I do not believe any serious attempt was made by Liberal members of the main committee to understand the reports of subcommittees from any other province but their own.

There has been gerrymandering, Mr. Chairman, and there have

Redistribution
been glaring inequalities created by the proposed redistribution. I propose now to refer specifically to some of these. I do not intend to confine my remarks to one province.
History does repeat itself, Mr. Chairman. Those of us who were in the house at the time of the last redistribution in 1947 will recall the pattern followed at that time. It was not without significance that the ridings selected for major operations by the government of the day were the ridings represented at that time by leading figures in the Progressive Conservative party. One recalls some of those major operations.
There was the case of Mr. Bracken, then leader of the party, who represented the riding of Neepawa. Next to him was a riding represented by another Progressive Conservative, the riding of Portage la Prairie. What could be more obvious than linking those together? And that was done. Then, there was the financial critic for the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Macdon-nell), representing then the riding of Muskoka-Ontario. What could be more obvious than to liquidate him by annexing that riding to another? That was done. There was also the hon. member for Lake Centre. At that time a major operation was performed upon his riding. I think it is a great tribute to him that, in spite of the difficulties put in his path by those who were responsible for redistribution in 1947, he came out of the 1949 election with an even greater majority than in 1945. This was in spite of the best efforts of those redistribution surgeons who went to work on his riding in 1947. Then there was the hon. member for Kamloops, who was also singled out for a major operation. One could cite many others. The pattern became familiar, and what we have in 1952 is largely a repetition in that certain prominent members of this party have been singled out for special attention by the Liberal surgeons. It may be something of a compliment to be selected for this class, because the class is outstanding.
Let me review briefly the fate of some of those who have been marked out for special attention. I begin with the province of Saskatchewan. Again the riding of Lake Centre has been singled out for special attention. We see that when the major operation has been performed, the riding of Lake Centre has had removed from it no fewer than 90 townships. There remain 102 townships, but the operation does not end there. There has been added to this riding the whole of the city of Moose Jaw, with a population of some 25,000, as well as 25 other townships. Further, there have been added, from the city of Regina itself, 3,600 people off the

riding of Qu'Appelle, and from the outskirts of the city of Regina itself 6,000 people have been added. According to the report of the committee, this makes a total for this riding of 56,800 people. With the exception of the urban riding of Regina, this rural riding is by a considerable measure the most populous of all ridings in Saskatchewan.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that is not the only consideration. It is not simply population and size, but the question of access which has to be considered. As most hon. members are aware, the riding of Lake Centre is bisected by Last Mountain lake, which is a serious impediment to access in that riding. It is quite possible in that riding to be ten miles from some place across the lake and have to go ninety miles around the lake to reach it. However, when the Saskatchewan Liberal surgeons had completed their surgery, we find Moose Jaw-Lake Centre to be one of the largest ridings in area and the largest in population outside of the city of Regina. We see interesting comparisons with some of the ridings around it. For instance, here is Qu'Appelle with a population of approximately 41,000; here is the riding of Melville with a population of 42,300. Both of those are smaller in area than the riding of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. Then there is the riding of Yorkton with 48,300, and a still smaller area than the riding of Muskoka-Lake Centre.

The riding of Digby-Yarmouth, with Barrington municipality included, would have had a population of 49,356. The riding of Digby-Annapolis-Kings now has a population of 66,510; the riding of Queens-Lunenburg a population of 45,800; and the riding of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare a population of 45,595. It is one of the smallest ridings in northern Ontario in population; it does not begin to compare in population with some of the large ridings in northern Ontario.
Hon. members may have their own ideas about the modern definition of pocket boroughs, but I am suggesting that simply because an hon. member of this house happens to be a minister is no reason for extending favourable consideration to him. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say something about this present system of redistribution. First of all, I would point out that there is a complete lack of principle in dealing with this redistribution across Canada. As has been mentioned in other debates, concessions have been given to Prince Edward Island in that they can never go below their Senate representation which gives them four seats. With less than 100,000 population it means that there are four constituencies with less than 25,000 population each. I am not objecting to that, but I do want to point out that differences do exist in certain parts of this country.
One of the first things this committee did was to bring in the formula known as the 15 per cent formula which provided that no province should lose more than 15 per cent of its constituencies as a result of the change in population as shown by the last census.
[Mr Fleming.]
An amendment was moved that the formula should be 10 per cent, but that amendment was voted down on a partisan basis. Every member supporting the government voted down that amendment. Had the amendment been adopted it would have assured three extra seats on the prairies, one for Manitoba, one for Saskatchewan and one for Alberta. By not adopting the amendment three voices which could speak on behalf of those provinces were eliminated. That was a most important move by the committee.
It will thus be seen that we are not following a genuine principle across the country in an effort to achieve representation by population. It now means that Manitoba loses two seats and Saskatchewan loses three. Manitoba has gained in population in the last ten years while Saskatchewan has fallen off. The result is that it will require an average of 6,400 more population for a constituency in Manitoba to elect a member than will be required in Saskatchewan. That is a rather unfair situation to exist in two provinces situated side by side. As I say, one province has increased considerably in population while the other has faced a considerable decrease in population.
A great deal has been said by previous speakers about the way in which redistribution has been carried out across the country. As I pointed out, we had to lose two seats in my province. I was a member of the committee and I do not think we followed any general principle as to what seats should be eliminated. I do not think those two seats should have been taken from the opposition. We are losing one seat in central Manitoba which, as has been pointed out, has the largest population of any rural seat in the province. If it was right to take away one seat in the central part of the province, then I think that should have been followed by taking two seats.
The other seat was Souris, which has a small population. It is a corner riding. Irrespective of the stories that we have heard in the past, the first consideration of the committee when it met was whether the constituency of Lisgar should be eliminated. That is, we would take two corner seats, both of which were small in population, and make two seats rather than three in southern Manitoba. However, we got into an argument about racial origins and matters of that sort and it was decided that we could not proceed on that basis. It was decided we could not proceed on that basis but that was the first proposition. There were several counter-proposals discussed before the committee. As the result of all these discussions the proposal was adopted by a majority vote that in the

case of Souris some 84 townships should be joined with 53 townships of Brandon, including the city of Brandon which has a population of 20,000, thus giving a population of 54,784 to the new Brandon-Souris constituency. I think one should keep in mind that the number of townships involved is 137 because a comparison was made this morning by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, I believe, of St. Boniface and Brandon-Souris, and he mentioned how well it had worked out.
Before referring to that comparison I might say that there are another 31 townships of Brandon which will now be in Marquette constituency, and the other 18 townships of Souris are to be taken into the constituency of Lisgar. However, when anybody compares the proposed constituency of Brandon-Souris with St. Boniface I should like to point out that the city of St. Boniface has a population of some 26,000, 6,000 greater than the city of Brandon. The constituency of St. Boniface will now have approximately 33 townships including the city of St. Boniface compared with 137 in Brandon-Souris. The population of St. Boniface constituency will be 52,218 or only 2,500 less than Brandon-Souris. Surely there is no principle of parity there as to either area or population. I think the set-up of these two ridings is most unfair from the point of view of either area or population.
Several of the counter-proposals would have produced a much better looking map than is now the case so far as the map of Manitoba is concerned. With respect to the central ridings, part of the present riding of Selkirk is now to be included in Portage-Neepawa. If one wishes to leave Winnipeg to drive to Riding Mountain national park and Clear lake one will follow Portage avenue or St. James street and at the outskirts of the city one enters the riding of Portage-Neepawa which at that point is some eighteen to twenty miles across from north to south. When you reach Poplar Point on No. 1 highway there is a narrow neck in the constituency where it is less than six miles wide north and south. Then you enter an area which extends to a great distance north and south, and if you follow highway No. 1 to Carberry and drive north to Riding Mountain national park and Clear lake you cover a distance of almost 200 miles. On the map Portage-Neepawa has a very peculiar appearance. I admit that the community of interest is east and west and that one travels mainly east and west, but I do say that political considerations have certainly played a great part in the majority report presented on behalf of the Manitoba subcommittee.
Redistribution
I think the same thing can be said of several other provinces but I want to point out particularly what I think is a very great disparity between what now may be considered the urban-rural ridings of St. Boniface and Brandon-Souris. Again I repeat that I think it was quite unnecessary to deal with the ridings of Souris and Brandon as they have been dealt with in this instance. From the points of view of geography and representation I do not think there has been equality of treatment, and again I am bound to agree with those who say there has been considerable gerrymandering in the redefining of boundaries in the province of Manitoba.

The Liberal party looked around and determined that these two members should also be taught a lesson. Unfortunately, there were no large handy blocks of C.C.F. votes to put in these ridings to help to eliminate the two present members, and the Liberal members in the adjoining ridings were not willing to give up Liberal votes to help defeat them. What did the Liberal party do? They simply joined the two ridings involved with two other Conservative ridings, in the hope that in the nominations for the combined ridings, the offending members would be eliminated.
That is the kind of thing that has been taking place with respect to redistribution, and those are three reasons why redistribution by an independent impartial commission is an absolute must if we are ever going to have the job done on a fair and equitable basis.

speechtext:
I was not a member of the redistribution committee, but I am told by those who were members of the subcommittees that in several cases the subcommittees did not at all resemble democratic committees; where

people present their case; are heard in a democratic way; have the pros and cons of their case listened to; and receive a fair deal. In several cases, these committees were far more like kangaroo courts, with the decision made ahead of time, and the maps drawn before the committee even met. I think that is the kind of procedure that should be reserved for dictatorship. It is the sort of thing that happens in dictatorships, and the fact that the practice is creeping more and more into the way things are done by this government is, I think, very, regrettable indeed. We have democratic institutions and ways of doing things, of which we are proud, and I am sorry to see that we seem to be slipping away from that democratic way and getting more and more into the dictatorial way.
I just have one last hope, and I suppose it is a last hope, that some of these real injustices will be reconsidered before this bill is passed, and that in the interests of fair play and good government these wrongs will be righted.
