In view of the speech by the hon. member for Broadview I think perhaps I ought to take a few moments of the time of the committee to try to clarify some matters with respect to Ontario.
It is not always an easy job, of course, to deal with redistribution in a committee. I believe it is only fair that the house should be told that the smallest constituency in Ontario at the present time is Glengarry. When hon. members talk about historic constituencies and so on, it is probably well to realize that that county has had a very outstanding history. If the remarks about the great history of any county are to be applied to other counties, they certainly should be applied to that one. This constituency happens to be represented today by a Liberal. I think the term used by the opposition is a "distinguished" Liberal-certainly I think a distinguished and outstanding Liberal-but in any event that is the first constituency you deal with in Ontario.
This constituency was joined with the fourth smallest constituency in the province, Prescott. Prescott had a population of 25,576, and that is a constituency with a very fine history, too. It is a constituency represented in this house by a Liberal member. I do not understand why the opposition always pick out only one or two illustrations upon which to make their case. If they have an argument, surely they should deal with the whole matter. These two, the first and fourth smallest constituencies, were joined together. It is a most difficult and frankly embarrassing thing to agree to having them joined together,

but it is the fair and proper thing to do in all the circumstances.
Now then, the second smallest constituency in the province of Ontario is Haldimand. Much has been said about that historic county today. Abutting Haldimand on the one side is the constituency of Welland. A new constituency has been created there, but nothing has been said by the opposition about that new constituency so far. Not only that; another constituency that was mentioned a great deal this morning was Brant-Went-worth, represented in the house by an opposition member. This constituency extends from the city of Hamilton to the city of Brantford. Not quite half of its population was put in with a portion of the population of the present constituency of Wentworth, and the remainder was joined together with the second smallest constituency in the province. Naturally it is a matter of regret that there are two sitting members of the opposition party representing those two constituencies.
I understand the feelings of the opposition members on that point, but those feelings are no greater than the feelings of other parties when these things arise, including the party in power at the moment. It is unfortunate that the present member for Brant-Wentworth lives in that part of his constituency that will be in Haldimand, if the suggestion now before the committee should be carried out. It is unfortunate, but the fact remains that the argument would have been completely destroyed if he had lived in that part of his constituency which is in the city of Hamilton. The argument is based on the residence of the sitting member, and not on a question of joining counties. It is unfortunate, and I am quite frank to say that I do not like the idea of the constituencies of the members being joined together like that, but under the circumstances I think it is the fair and proper thing to do.
The next constituency which has been mentioned is that of Wellington North. It is the third smallest, and I shall come back to it in a moment. The fourth smallest is Prescott, and I have mentioned what happened to it. The next one is Huron North. Huron North and Wellington North abut each other, and an attempt was made to work out something that would join those two together. As the hon. member for Huron North will be the first to agree, I think, it is not proper at all to do that, having in mind the layout of the counties and the surveys. It is not a proper way of approaching the thing. The surveys in that area, incidentally, are rather peculiar, and the boundaries of these old historic counties are quite curious because of the fact the surveys have different fronts.

I think the hon. member for Lanark is reasonably familiar with the road situation and I believe he will agree with me if I go so far as to say that the road situation is rather bad in that area and that it is a fairly inaccessible area.
I have dealt with the six smallest constituencies and shown how they have been combined. Perhaps I should take the largest constituencies and show what has been done with them. There was one matter of some embarrassment; that was the city of Toronto. As everyone knows who deals with the city of Toronto, there is a question as to whether or not that city is over-represented. We passed that matter by and I think we were right in doing that, in all the circumstances. But I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Broadview, of all people, arguing the merits of redistribution in Ontario this afternoon; because if there is one thing that is self evident in Toronto it is that the area east of the Don river these three constituencies of Broadview, Greenwood and Danforth do fairly well on population figures, if you are talking about the elimination of constituencies. In any event, we agreed not to do that.
I think there is a situation there which, in fairness to the house, could not be overlooked; and I think we arrived at something that was quite workable. We took the smallest one, namely the constituency of Danforth in the city of Toronto and added
27,000	of population from the township of 
Scarborough immediately abutting that constituency. That procedure does not in any way do any violence to the road system. It is the back area immediately adjacent to Danforth. That is what was done there. In any event, I now revert to my former point, namely of taking the largest constituencies and dealing with them one by one.
The largest constituency in the province was York East with a population of 159,000. Of that number 27,000 were taken and joined to Danforth, the smallest city seat in Toronto. The remainder was divided approximately in two; and I think there can be no charge of unfairness with regard to our. dealing with that constituency.
The next largest constituency is York West, with a population of 126,000. That was divided in two and I think there can be no charge of unfairness in the method of division. The two constituencies have a population within a thousand of each other.

It is 126,420. I will give the precise population of the new constituencies if I can find the sheet. The new constituency of York-Humber will have 64,480 and the new constituency of York West will have 63,816. I was overgenerous when I said there was a difference of almost 1,000; it is 600.
The next largest constituency is Welland. Its population was 123,233. Incidentally it is a constituency abutting on Haldimand. Instead of amalgamating the two, we divided Welland in two. I have not the figures with me at the moment, but it is an even division.
I think there can be no disagreement with the boundaries there.
The next largest constituency is York North, having a population of 122,538. That constituency was divided in two. The next largest constituency is Wentworth having a population of 119,728. That constituency, plus 750 of population that was in the former Brant-Wentworth constituency and was within the city of Hamilton, was divided in two, making a purely city constituency and another by putting together the remainder of Wentworth county that was in Wentworth constituency and the part of Wentworth county that was in Brant-Wentworth constituency. It seems to me that is the fair thing to do. That means Hamilton now has three wholly city seats and Wentworth county has one member with I think the right number of population in relation to a built-up county of that sort.
The next largest constituency was Sudbury. Subject to adjusting the population in order to meet the travel conditions with the two railway lines through the area, that constituency was divided in two; and I have not

heard a word of quarrelling or difference of opinion with respect to the division of that area.
The point I want to make is that I have shown how the six smallest constituencies were combined and the six largest constituencies were divided in two. It seems to me that point has not been dealt with by those criticizing the plan. The truth of the matter is that there cannot be much criticism within that field. The criticism I felt might be levelled at us is that maybe we did not go far enough, or that we should have continued and tried to readjust all constituencies. There are endless problems if you get into that field. However, I felt these things should be put on the record here in answer to the arguments of the opposition.
There may be things they want to say about particular constituencies, and I well understand their feelings with respect to particular members who happen to live in the areas being combined. Incidentally it arose only in one case as far as the official opposition is concerned, and in that case it arises only because of the fact that the hon. member happens to live in one part of his constituency. I would remind hon. members, when they speak so strongly on that point, that it is no less personally embarrassing and personally unpleasant to amalgamate constituencies which are wholly represented by Liberal members. It is no less embarrassing at all. I think the committee should realize that fact and deal with the matter on that basis.

Mr. Chairman, I think we have here an illustration of how redistribution should not be done. If ever a parliament had a demonstration of how it should not be done, this parliament is having one at the present moment. For example, I cannot understand why the constituency of Moose Jaw should include part of the suburbs of Regina as well as part of the city itself. would take responsibility for such a suggestion. Even at this late stage I think the parts of the city proper and the suburbs of Regina should be restored to Regina. As a matter of fact that would increase the population of that constituency to around 70,000 and the objection will be taken that 70,000 is above the quota set for constituencies under redistribution. There are 17 constituencies in the province of Ontario alone that have populations of 70,000 or over under the new proposed redistribution. There is one Nova Scotia seat which might be classified as rural, though there are some incorporated towns in it. I refer to the constituency of the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings, which will now be Digby-Annapolis-Kings. That has a population of pretty close to 70,000, over 66,000 anyway. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says the constituencies of Winnipeg North Centre, Winnipeg South Centre and the other Winnipeg constituencies are all 75,000 or over. Then what is the objection to doing the right, the proper, the intelligent and sensible thing and putting the suburbs of Regina where they belong, namely in the city of Regina? It is absurd to take the suburbs of a city and put that suburban area into a rural constituency. Other areas included in Moose Jaw are inside the Regina city limits; I am talking about what were once the suburbs. They are inside the city limits. To put areas inside the city limits of Regina into the constituency of Moose Jaw is an absurdity, and I can tell you that both the people of Moose Jaw and Regina will resent it, and will properly show their resentment a year or so from now, as they should.

I think it demonstrates that we should do what has been done in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand and several other countries, and turn over the matter of redistribution to an expert committee such as I suggested some years ago. I am not suggesting who the personnel of the committee should be, but I am suggesting the kind of committee when I say it should have a judge as chairman, and that as members of the commission there should be a statistician who could deal with figures, and a geographer or surveyor or whatever he would be called, to consider the topographical features of the countryside.

Mr. Chairman, this morning the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration indicated the number of constituencies in which changes had been made as 124 and those in which no change had been made as 130. He made quiet a point of the fact that in the case of approximately half the constituencies no change was being made. I think we all agree that where no change is necessary in order to equalize population
Redistribution
changes it is to the advantage of everybody that things should be left as they are. It disturbs people to be shifted around from one constituency to another and they do not like it.
It is rather noteworthy that as- far as Alberta is concerned this general principle, if it was one, which the minister attempted to indicate was followed, was not followed. In fact no attention was paid to it. The minister stated that 15 seats in Alberta were being changed with two remaining as they were. With the exception of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the greatest number of changes in constituencies is taking place in Alberta. In the case of Manitoba and Saskatchewan all constituencies are being changed.
This great number of changes is taking place in Alberta despite the fact that there is to be no change in the number of members from that province. We had 17 members before and we will have 17 members in the next parliament. In spite of that there were more changes than in any other province. In the case of Nova Scotia, where a seat is to be eliminated, there were fewer changes than in Alberta. Therefore it leads one to wonder why the Liberal majority on the Alberta subcommittee and on the main committee found it necessary to make all these changes in Alberta.
What has happened so far as the Calgary area is concerned is that boundaries that have been in existence in their present form since 1923, and to a large extent in their present form since 1911, have been completely done away with and other boundaries have been very materially changed. Something was said in the subcommittee about certain people having asked for a change. So far as I know none of the sitting members from the three seats covering various parts of the city of Calgary have received any complaints with regard to the existing set-up. I certainly did not receive any. The hon. member for Bow River, who was a member of that committee, stated that he had never received any. To my knowledge while the late Arthur Smith was the member for Calgary West he did not receive any, and the present member for Calgary West has certainly never said anything to me about having received any.
In spite of the fact that the three members representing that area were quite satisfied with the present set-up the Liberal majority on the committee insisted on destroying the present boundaries and changing things around more or less completely. The odd thing about it is that the city of Calgary under the present set-up has three constituencies each of which contains a part of the city of Calgary and has a rural area attached

Redistribution
to it. As it happens the population of these three constituencies added together is almost exactly the same as the population of the three new seats to be created in Edmonton by this redistribution. Edmonton formerly had two seats and an extra seat was added, giving an average population for the three new seats of about 61,000. Under the old setup the average population for the three Calgary seats is about the same.
There is also the fact that when Edmonton was divided into three seats the same principle was put into effect that has existed in Calgary for the last twenty years. In order to build up the population sufficiently to justify a third seat in Edmonton some of the rural areas surrounding the city were included, so in the city of Edmonton you have three seats with rural areas attached to each. It is quite true that one of these seats has a very small portion of rural area attached to it, but the other two have a fair amount. Therefore under this redistribution the same general set-up was put into effect in Edmonton that had existed in Calgary for some twenty years. However, in spite of that fact the set-up in Calgary was destroyed and the city of Calgary was reduced to two purely urban seats.
The result of that action is of course to make the population of the Calgary seats upwards of 8,000 greater on the average than that of the three Edmonton seats. There was no necessity to create any disparity in population between the seats in Calgary and Edmonton. If the existing set-up had been retained in Calgary the populations would have been almost exactly the same, but by putting a new set-up into effect in Calgary the result is that it takes 8,000 more people to elect a representative in Calgary than is the case in the city to the north.
So far as the Calgary area is concerned, redistribution could have been carried out quite simply and easily and, so far as I know, to the satisfaction of all the people of the southern part of the province, certainly to the satisfaction of the members now representing the people of Calgary. All that was necessary was to leave the existing set-up as it was, move the boundaries a few blocks to the west in order to equalize the population, and redistribution in that area would have been accomplished. The population would have been equalized and so far as I know everybody concerned would have been happy except the Liberal machine in Alberta. The only thing I can believe is that the members of that party have some far-fetched idea that by juggling things around in this way they are going to do themselves some good, but I do not think for a moment that will follow.

In order to accomplish the changing around of the Calgary area the constituency of Bow River had to be excluded completely from the city of Calgary. There was added to it all the rural area that had formerly been in Calgary West and some of the rural area that had been in Calgary East, with the result that under this plan you now have a constituency extending from the British Columbia boundary at Trail some 200 miles to the east to within 84 miles of the Saskatchewan boundary, thus creating an unnecessarily large constituency. There was no necessity to create a constituency of that size and at the same time create a disparity in population between it and the two Calgary seats of some 28,000. The population of the constituency of Bow River will be down to something over 40,000 while the two Calgary seats will have a population of just under 69,000.
All these things, which were contrary to the principles we have heard should be followed so far as redistribution is concerned, were done in order to get rid of the existing set-up in Calgary. I think one of the statements made when this matter was discussed in the main redistribution committee explains the matter. It was said there that the existing set-up had to go, that it was the result of gerrymandering in 1933 and that the situation was just not going to be allowed to continue as it was. I do not know how the constituencies were established in 1933 because I was not here. However, I know that the constituency of Calgary East, which was objected to particularly, happens to be an area which at that time contained and still contains, in a strip about a mile to a mile and a half wide running through the centre of the city, the bulk of the population. That is the area in which the greatest density of population is found. I do not think there is any question but that the constituencies were set up in that form in order to divide the population evenly and to avoid having overly large rural constituencies.
I think the fact the statement to which I have referred was made in the committee is the explanation why there was such insistence on destroying a set-up that had existed in Calgary for such a long period of time, and putting into effect an entirely new one. The only argument advanced against the existing arrangement and in favour of the plan proposed in the schedule now before us was that the existing set-up looked funny on the map. If you look at the map of any province you will see many very peculiar looking constituencies. In other words, the argument that it looks funny on the map means absolutely nothing. It was a ridiculous argument.

The only other argument put forward was that Calgary should be made into two purely urban constituencies because two urban constituencies would be preferable to the existing partly urban and partly rural constituencies. As I said in the committee, there is no magic in a purely urban constituency. All kinds of arguments can be advanced in favour of a constituency which is both urban and rural. I think those arguments carry more weight than the argument that a purely urban constituency should be created wherever it is possible to do so.
I think what we need in Canada is to get the people in the cities and in the country more closely together instead of trying to separate them by artificial means.
In order to indicate what is thought of this projected plan I should like to read a portion of an editorial which I just received today, and which appeared in the Calgary Albertan, a newspaper which has supported the Liberal party as long as I can remember. At the outset I might say that I believe this editorial could be summed up by saying that it condemns what has been done in the Calgary area by faint praise. The editorial says:
The juggling of Calgary and southern Alberta federal constituency boundaries makes sense, in general, although it is disturbing that the parliamentary Liberals, who have no representation in southern Alberta and therefore know nothing about the region, forced the changes over the objections of the members who do know the region.
This historic constituency of Calgary West, represented so Illustriously by the late R. B. Bennett and the late Arthur L. Smith, passes out of existence. But Calgary North and Calgary South will continue to send capable men to parliament, we may be sure.
Calgary is now split into three constituencies, Calgary East, Calgary West and Bow River. All three include considerable rural territory, and in the case of Bow River the rural section, including Drumheller, is actually in the majority. The new set-up strips all the rural territory away and leaves Calgary with two constituencies. Actually the city's representation Is not increased although it has grown much faster than the province generally.
In other words, we are under-represented. We were under-represented before, and that under-representation will be considerably greater now.
Population in each of the new city ridings is up to 20,000 higher than in the adjacent rural ridings, and that's not right.
As a matter of fact one area is up to
29,000	higher. The editorial continues:
Is it better to have one member represent both city people and country people, or to have a separate representative for each? This is a debatable point. If an M.P. is responsible to both farmers and city folk he will understand the problems of both of them better. And since they have to live together, so to speak, there will be less occupational cleavage. On the other hand there may be a tendency, when one member represents

The new Bow River constituency will stretch from Drumheller to British Columbia. That makes it something of a geographical monstrosity. But over most of that territory the population is sparse, and some other constituencies are even larger.
The original Calgary constituency was created in 1903 and split in 1914, while Mr. Bennett was the member, into East and West. Calgary West is regarded as a Conservative stronghold. Calgary East, on the other hand, is good fighting ground for almost any party. Since 1917 it has been represented by Labour, Liberal, Conservative and Social Credit members. The current Conservative hold is precarious.

I might say there has been no change in the distribution of seats in Alberta since 1933. In connection with the first problem I mentioned, the constituencies _ of Acadia, Battle River, Camrose and Vegreville were all low in population. It was agreed to make three constituencies out of the four; and because of the tremendous increase in the population of the city of Edmonton, it was necessary to set up a third seat there. All these changes, by the way, received the unanimous approval of the subcommittees, so I do not need to spend any time over them except to point out that it was because of this situation that there were so many changes in boundaries of constituencies in Alberta.
The problem of correcting the situation in the Calgary area was not so easy, and I may say we did not have the same unanimous approval. Formerly the city of Calgary was divided into three parts known as Calgary East, Calgary West and Bow River. The constituency of Bow River took in the eastern part of the city together with 96 townships of the rural areas. The former riding of Calgary East consisted of a narrow corridor extending from the north to the south through the centre of the city. In one section this corridor is only seven blocks wide, and it is only 16 blocks wide in its widest part. It has also had attached to it a rural area of 52 townships extending from the city of Calgary west to the British Columbia border. Calgary West did have the western portion of the city at least to justify its name, but it also included 96 townships of rural area extending again from Calgary west to the British Columbia border.
The committee decided to set up two urban Calgary seats made up of the city proper, together with certain suburbs, to be known as Calgary North and Calgary South. The rural part of Bow River, together with the former rural area of Calgary West and a small portion from Medicine Hat, will now constitute the constituency of Bow River, which will be a rural constituency.
Changes made in Macleod, Lethbridge and Medicine Hat were all of a minor nature to equalize population.

The hon. member for Calgary East regrets the loss of what he termed the historic constituency of Calgary West. I might say it was on his recommendation that Calgary was divided east and west, thus constituting the constituencies of Calgary South and Calgary North. As convener of the subcommittee, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that these changes are justified and reasonable.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure all hon. members will agree it is very strange that although we have had a debate extending over two-thirds of this day, nothing has yet been said about British Columbia. It is time to rectify that situation.

I would like to have as much hope that the proposed map of British Columbia might be rectified; but from what I have heard before, I think that is a forlorn hope. Nevertheless there are certain observations with respect to the proposals being made in British Columbia which I think should be drawn to the attention of the committee, in the hope that the same sort of wrong principle which I maintain has been followed in that province on this occasion may not be followed there at a later time.
All the arguments which have been heard today and the arguments I intend to put forward with respect to British Columbia do, I maintain, further reinforce the suggestion that instead of having redistribution carried out by a committee of members of parliament, with the inevitable manoeuvring and counter-manoeuvring and political considerations which must enter into the matter, it should be carried out by an independent commission which could look at the task impartially and report to parliament its recommendations so we might give our final approval.
This time we are to have four new seats in British Columbia. This means that our membership will increase from 18 to 22 members, or almost 25 per cent over the present number. This gives us an opportunity, or at least should give us an opportunity, which is unique, that of looking at the map of our province and placing therein the constituencies on a scientific and impartial basis so as to properly represent those areas having a community of interest, while at the same time relieving some of the bad features in the present distribution of constituencies in British Columbia, by reducing certain constituencies from their present enormous size- a factor which makes it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to represent those areas adequately.
But, instead of that, a Liberal majority on the subcommittee-and in this respect we have been in exactly the same situation as every other provincial subcommittee-decided there should be an arbitrary allocation of

seats, one to the lower mainland area surrounding Vancouver, one to Vancouver island, one to the interior of the province and the fourth to the city of Vancouver.
As it happens I have no quarrel, in general, with the first three suggestions. But I maintain that the population figures of our province are such that there is no justification for placing one of the new seats within the city limits of Vancouver. I start with the fact that the national quotient obtained by dividing the population of Canada by the proposed number of seats in the House of Commons is approximately 54,000. I am told by the chief electoral officer that it has been traditionally recognized in Canada, as well as in other commonwealth countries- indeed, I believe he went so far as to say it is recognized in every democratic country with a system of representative government- that there should be a differential between the population average for city ridings and the population average for country ridings. The reason of course is obvious, namely that if one were to insist upon absolute equality of population between rural and urban ridings, rural ridings would cover areas which individual members would find it impossible adequately to represent. On the other hand, in the city ridings population is confined within a reasonably small geographical area.
I am told further that the average margin of tolerance in respect of the differential between city and rural ridings runs at a maximum of from 20 to 25 per cent. If one takes 20 per cent of 54,000, or approximately
11.000	he gets an average for city ridings of 65,000. If one were to apply the maximum of 25 per cent it would become permissible to raise the population of city ridings to 67,500, which would be 13,500 over the national quotient.
If you take the population figures for British Columbia and divide them by the number of seats now proposed to be given to that province, namely 22, you will find that the average provincial quotient works out to 52,964, or in round figures 53,000. Then if we divide the population of Vancouver by the proposed number of seats it is now to get-that is, six seats instead of five-we find the proposed average for city ridings in Vancouver is 57,856, or just about 5,000 over the provincial quotient and only about
4.000	over the national quotient. On the other hand the average for the remainder of the seats outside the city of Vancouver would then be 51,130.
We get the result therefore that under the proposed arrangement the city of Vancouver will have an average of 57,856 while the

remainder of the province will have an average of 51,130, or a differential of only 6,726 between seats in the city of Vancouver and those in the rest of the province.
I am not going to maintain that all the seats in the rest of the province are rural, because that is not correct; but for the purposes of my argument I confine my attention to the city of Vancouver. Let me say that all the people of British Columbia, including those in the interior of the province from which I come, are proud of the city of Vancouver. We know it is the finest city in Canada, and that so far as cities are concerned it should be entitled to the maximum possible representation.
But when you compare the present proposal as it affects Vancouver with the proposals for the other major cities in Canada, you find that not only is the differential between city seats in Vancouver and the rest of the province too low, but that the average size of the city seats in Vancouver is very considerably less than the average size of the seats in practically every other major city in Canada.
I gave the figure for the city of Vancouver on the present proposed basis as 57,856. Looking at the proposals as they will affect the other cities of Canada we find that the city of Winnipeg has an average for its constituencies of 76,945, or almost 20,000 more than the city of Vancouver. Incidentally in that connection we heard this morning the hon. member for Winnipeg South justifying that large population average for the city of Winnipeg by saying he recognized that there should be a differential, against the city ridings. You will remember that I asked him to advance the same argument to the chairman of the British Columbia subcommittee, but unfortunately he declined to do so.
When you come to Ontario you find that the average for the Toronto seats is 64,000; the average for the York seats will be just under 70,000, and the average for the Toronto and York seats will be approximately 65,300, as against the average of 57,856 for the Vancouver seats. The average for the seats on the island of Montreal, which are not all city seats, is 65,000. The average for the seats in Calgary is 69,000. In every case the proposed average for Vancouver is substantially less than the average of any other city in Canada, and is only a little more than the average of all the seats in British Columbia, the vast majority of which are rural and which have a pressing problem resulting from their enormous geographical areas from which they require relief.

It has been my contention, and still is, that instead of that one extra seat within the city limits of Vancouver there should be two seats on the lower mainland outside of Vancouver. Not only would this give necessary relief to the lower mainland area-which now does not get the relief it should have and which is still going to have the New Westminster riding with approximately 81,000 people, and the two Burnaby ridings still very large-not only does the confinement of one seat within the city limits of Vancouver mean that the lower mainland area does not get the relief it should have, it means that there are not enough seats left to bring relief to the constituencies in the interior of the province which now have such huge areas.
If the proper principle had been adopted and two seats allotted to the lower mainland area it would have enabled the moving back northward and eastward of the boundaries of the seats immediately surrounding Vancouver, including Fraser Valley and Coast-Capilano; and that, with one seat going to the interior, would have enabled real relief to be given by adjusting the boundaries of the interior ridings of the province so as to make manageable constituencies.
As a result of the insistence of the majority of the subcommittee that their proposals be followed, we are left with the riding of Vancouver Centre with a population of between 47,500 and 48,000, one of the smallest city ridings in all Canada. There you have a population of 48,000 in an area of perhaps five square miles at the most. In contrast you have constituencies with 49,000, in the case of Kootenay West, approximately 40,000 in the case of Cariboo and 45,000 in the new riding of Kamloops which ridings cover areas of as much as at least 50,000 square miles on the average. On the one hand you have
40,000	people and an area of 50,000 square miles, and on the other hand you have 47,500 people and an area of 5 square miles. That is the sort of ridiculous situation you arrive at when you follow the wrong principle which the Liberal majority on the subcommittee has been following.
Just in passing it does seem to me that if they are going to do anything in Vancouver; if they are going to insist upon putting an extra seat in there, surely the time has arrived to adjust that situation and bring up the population of Vancouver Centre to something approaching that of the other city ridings.
Another result of the proposal of the majority on the subcommittee is in connection with Revelstoke. At present Revelstoke is in the Kamloops federal riding. I believe the people are reasonably satisfied to be there. I

Redistribution
have had no substantial complaints from that area against their being in the Kamloops riding, although representations have been made from time to time that the Revelstoke district has its community of interest, both geographically and economically, with the Kootenay country.
When the subject of redistribution was first discussed this year I received representations to the effect that the time had arrived when it should be considered whether Revelstoke should now be placed back in one of the Kootenay constituencies. In fact they named the constituency of Kootenay West. I replied that I did not consider that that was essential; that if it were done it would mean that the populations of Kootenay West and Kamloops, instead of being practically equal as at present, would be changed so that Kootenay West would be increased and Kamloops would be reduced, thus producing an inequality. But I did say that if any change were made with respect to Revelstoke it was my view that it should go into the Kooter*ay constituency where its community of interest lay.
Then as to the needed relief in the interior of our province; because there is to be only one new riding there, instead of further relief being afforded by way of two ridings on the lower mainland outside of Vancouver, as I have suggested; since there is to be only one new riding, all you can do in the face of the present figures is to divide the present riding of Yale, which has a population of nearly 80,000. But that would create a situation where you would have two constituencies of some 39,000 each, both with much smaller areas and substantially smaller in population than the next door riding of Kamloops, and about the same population as, but an infinitely smaller area than, Cariboo and Skeena, both the latter having less population than Kamloops.
It began to be felt by the majority of the committee that that would not be fair, that Yale should not be divided exactly in half but that a line would have to be run slightly north of centre. Then in order to bring the population of the northern half of the riding up to a point where it would compare with the southern half and the surrounding constituencies, it was suggested that Revelstoke should be added to the new North Okanagan seat. That has been done, with the result that instead of it being included in the Kootenay West riding as it should have been if a change was to be made at all-that is where the majority of the people wanted it to go-it is being artificially included in an Okanagan riding.
While it is true that Revelstoke is a lovely city with a beautiful golf course to which
[Mr. Fulton.1
the people from the Okanagan area come over the week end; while it is true that they have joint curling matches, the fact is that being on the main line of the C.P.R., being a lumbering and mining area, that district has practically no community of economic interest with the Okanagan area. But it is being artificially taken from that area to which it belongs and is being included in the Okanagan riding, an artificiality created as a result of the improper limitation of one of the extra seats to the city of Vancouver.
This is about all I propose to say with respect to our province, except to say that it is regrettable that the same practice was followed in connection with British Columbia as apparently was followed in every other provincial subcommittee. I refer to the fact that although there were some general discussions, there was no discussion of detail; yet maps began to appear in the press which must have been inspired from somewhere, and which were stated to have been approved by the British Columbia subcommittee. They were released before the details were considered, and in some cases before the general principle concerning some of the ridings had ever been discussed in the subcommittee. That is particularly the case with respect to the first details released of the new riding in the city of Vancouver. The proposal, about which we first learned through these articles in the press, was to put a new riding in the city of Vancouver by making it stretch the whole way from the east boundary to the west boundary of the city, a perfectly ridiculous and absurd proposition. I wish you could see from this distance, Mr. Chairman, the way the thing looks on the map then released. We have heard various descriptions of this practice this afternoon. We have heard the expressions "gerrymandering" and "jimmymandering". The leader of the opposition said this morning that the word "gerrymander" originated in the resemblance of the proposal to a reptile, the salamander. This riding looks almost exactly like a salamander.
There is one other thing it resembles even more closely than a salamander. It starts with a long thin strip out in the west end of Vancouver, the Point Grey area, a curved strip which might be said to resemble a fairly convenient handle. Then it narrows into a long straight thin strip-I believe in one place to be only seven blocks wide- right across the centre of the city until it comes within a short distance of the east boundary-

The constituency of Iles-de-la-Madeleine was created a federal riding in the redistribution of 1948, only four years ago. The house decided at that time that it should have its own representation in the House of Commons. Since that time the population of that county has increased. The reasons that existed at that time for giving it a representative of its own exist today; indeed, I shall try to show hon. members that they exist to an even greater extent now than they did at that time. Those who were on the redistribution committee in 1947 or 1948-I am not quite sure of the year -have told me there were three reasons why the Magdalen islands were made a constituency in their own right. These were ethnic, economical and geographic reasons.
The ethnic reason was that it was felt that the Acadians, the French-speaking citizens of Canada in the maritime provinces, did not have the representation they should have in the House of Commons. It is known that on the Magdalen islands 90 per cent of the people are French-speaking, and they are all of Acadian stock. It was felt therefore that they should be given an opportunity to be represented in the House of Commons by a French-speaking member.
The economic reason is that, although it is a small county, it is the county in my province in which there are the most fishermen. No other county in the whole of Quebec has more fishermen than have the Magdalen islands. As fishermen they have special problems, and it was felt that if they were left to form a part of another county, as they were when they formed part of the constituency of Gaspe, their member would not have time to give the amount of attention their problems require.
Hon. members may have noticed that during my membership in the House of Commons I have endeavoured to take a particular interest in the fisheries, and have tried to do what I could to improve the lot of the fishermen, by getting them harbours, wharves and breakwaters, with the assistance anJ.

Redistribution
good will of my good friend the Minister of Public Works. These are the economic reasons for which the county was created.
There was also a geographical reason. As you know, this constituency is situated out in the middle of the gulf of St. Lawrence, far from any other land. It is more than a hundred miles from Gaspe and about the same distance from Newfoundland. There were only two counties to which it could have been joined. One of these was the county of Gaspe to which it was attached before. Gaspe already has a population of over 60,000, and hon. members will have noted that the average population for constituencies stands at 54,000. The other county to which it could have been attached was the county of Saguenay. But that county, too, has a comparatively large population. It is far removed from the Magdalen islands, and to have attached the Magdalen islands to the county of Saguenay would not have been a practical procedure at all. Perhaps I might draw the attention of the committee to the fact that both of these counties, Gaspe and Saguenay, are at this time experiencing a large increase in population. Through the discoveries of copper in Gaspe and iron ore in Saguenay, considerable development is taking place in those counties. Because of that they now have a considerable population, and because of the additional development which is increasing their population it would not have been practical to attach the Magdalen islands to either of them.
I submit therefore that the reasons that existed in 1948 when the constituency was created exist now with even greater weight. As we are nearing the end of the session- we hope-I shall not detain the committee longer. However, I did wish to set out these reasons which, I suggest, are good and valid reasons why my constituency should be left as it is. I submit that the committee on redistribution for these reasons did well not to interfere with the status of the Magdalen islands; and the suggestion that the government and the Liberal party were at fault in allowing such a comparatively small group to be represented by their own member in the house is unfounded. I wish to set the record straight, and to reject any such suggestion.

On the general subject of the debate let me say that, as a new member in the house and in my first parliament, I have found it interesting to listen to what has been said in this debate on redistribution. While listening to it, however, I could not help thinking that much the same debate must take place at every redistribution after every census. My thoughts go back to 1932, when the Conservative party were in power and made the redistribution in their own way. At that time accusations of gerrymandering were made against them by the Liberal party, which was then in opposition.
I cannot help thinking that if members of the opposition are really sincere when they say they believe the problem of redistribution should be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons and referred to a commission they should explain why they did not do it when they were in power. My personal opinion is that the problem of representation in the House of Commons and the problem of the divisions with respect to the different federal constituencies is a matter that should remain in the hands of the House of Commons.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Some of the ministers do not think so.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that after listening to this debate, as you have, for the last several hours you must agree with me that this is about ^s weird a way of carrying on redistribution as anyone could very well imagine. One hon. member has described it as an abomination. Others have used other language. But what they all say amounts to this, that in the House of Commons we should find a better method than the one we are now using of carrying out a redistribution of seats in the Dominion of Canada.
I have not taken part in the debate up to this point because I have been waiting to see if I could make out any principle the government was following in the matter of redistribution. It seemed to me that they would have some general principle they would be following across the dominion. I was surprised when the hon. member for Ottawa West told us about the principle they had followed in the Ontario subcommittee, when he said that they had taken the six smallest constituencies and had added to them, and taken the six largest constituencies and subtracted from them. They had divided some of them, taken parts out of others, and

tried to get some equality so far as representation by population is concerned.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: But not very much.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
But after they had looked after the six smallest and the six largest constituencies, or at least had done something about them, they seemed to throw up their hands and pretty much accepted the others. That principle certainly was not carried out in Nova Scotia. I was a member of that subcommittee and there we found that one of the largest rural constituencies in Canada, if not the largest instead of being reduced or left as it was had another 12,000 added to it. I refer to Annapolis-Kings, to which Digby was added. They have created one of the largest rural constituencies in the Dominion of Canada.
When we came to Saskatchewan they took the largest constituency there, divided it into four and distributed it among the other constituencies in the area, putting them in the position where they had from 8,000 to 10,000 more population than many of the other rural constituencies in the province.
Down in Nova Scotia they have another principle which they follow, the shore line principle. That is a new one. I did not know that members represented shore lines; I thought they represented people. They told us in the subcommittee that a member could have only so many miles of shore line in his constituency and therefore they had to take some of the shore line out of Queens-Shelburne or one of the other constituencies down there and place it in Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
When we get out to Saskatchewan we find that the hon. member for Lake Centre has a lot of shore line in his constituency. He has a lake running right up through it. However, the shore line principle was not followed in Saskatchewan; in fact they had no principle to follow out there. They followed the Minister of Agriculture. I think he is a poor man to follow as far as redistribution is concerned.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: A poor substitute.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
A poor substitute for principle. For many years the Minister of Agriculture has been following a narrow line between truth and fiction. As he gets older the line gets more faded and he wanders off into the realm of fiction more and more. The result is that we have a pretty weird redistribution as far as Saskatchewan is concerned.
I think it is ridiculous the way this redistribution has been carried on. In Saskatchewan we find three constituencies up in

the northeast corner of the province, Hum-boldt-Melfort with 53,500; Prince Albert with 56,000 and Mackenzie with 49,600. Any hon. member looking at the map will realize that that is a new area. It contains a considerable acreage of land which is being taken out of the forest reserve and placed under cultivation every year. subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Why is the population less than it was in the last ten years?

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I am not talking about what happened in the last ten years, I am talking about what is likely to happen in the next ten years. That is the trouble with the Liberals, they are always looking backward, they do not look ahead. This is the only really new area in the province. It is being opened up and a large population is being placed in each constituency.
Then down in the southeast corner of the province we find the constituency of Moose Mountain with 41,300. There is the constituency of Qu'Appelle with a population of 42,500. Then there is Melville, represented by the Minister of Agriculture, with 43,500. After looking at the map one realizes that the only principle they could have followed in Saskatchewan was that the constituency of Melville must not be interfered with, or as little as possible; the constituencies north and south were to be maintained. After that anything could happen, and pretty nearly anything did happen so far as representation by population in that province is concerned.
I was on the Saskatchewan subcommittee for the 1947 redistribution. The present leader of the opposition in Saskatchewan was on that committee. He drew a map, just as the Liberal members of the subcommittee drew one this year. I said then, and I say now, that at least he followed some principle. The principle he followed was to try to maintain representation by population in the province with a variation of not more than 10 per cent. He carried that out pretty well, but this time that principle has been thrown to the winds. Apparently the Minister of Agriculture does not believe in it, or the committee does not believe in it. I do not know on whom to place the blame. The indications before the election, according to the press, were that the constituency of Assiniboia was to be eliminated. Apparently

Redistribution
the election results changed the minds of certain people and they decided to do it another way. So we find the constituency of Swift Current taken out and the constituency of Assiniboia again on the map. I think it is a fairer map than it would have been had they carried out the original intention.
This whole redistribution, not only as it concerns Saskatchewan but as it affects the other provinces as well, has apparently been built around individuals rather than around the basic principle of representation by population, representation to conform with the geographical areas to be represented.
In the constituency of Melfort, which was taken out, we had a constituency consisting of the drainage area in the northeastern part of the province from the Carrot and Saskatchewan rivers. The people who have gone into that area during the last 30 or 40 years have similar ideas and carried on similar pursuits. I think that constituency should have been left on the map. But it is taken out and the population redistributed, with the result that we do not have representation by population in the province of Saskatchewan. All we have is a mess. I think any honest person who looks at the map will agree with me.
When I was speaking in the main committee on this subject I mentioned that the population of the new constituency of Hum-boldt-Melfort would be some 53,500. At that time the hon. member for Rosthern rose and said, "Yes, but you have three towns in there, Humboldt, Melfort and Tisdale; besides that, the people in the area have large families." Just why people with large families should not have the same representation as people with small families is something I do not know. Apparently that is another new theory in redistribution which has been developed.
There you have it. The most weird excuses have been given for this map which has been described by some as an abomination. I could refer to the constituency of Lake Centre, but I am going to leave that to be dealt with by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I know he is quite capable of doing that. The whole thing is simply ridiculous. I do not think anyone can make out an honest case for what has been done in Saskatchewan. I am not going to deal with the other provinces except Nova Scotia, because I sat on that subcommittee. Exactly the same performance took place there. The thing is ridiculous. You have the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings with 66,510, and then a constituency right alongside represented by the worthy Minister of Resources and Development having 20,000 people less. I like the Minister of Resources
[Mr. Wright. 1
and Development, but why should he represent 20,000 fewer people than the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings? It just does not make sense. Therefore I hope that we can all agree at the next session or the one following that to do away with this method of redistribution. It is so ridiculous that one only has to talk about it to see people smile. I am sure if people throughout the country were listening to this performance, of if they read Hansard, they would be a bit disgusted with the method we are following at the present time. If we want democracy, if we want representation by population, then let us do something different from what we are doing now.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, being one of those members who has fallen out of favour with the present government, I hope that I may have an opportunity of speaking for a few minutes this evening on this extremely important matter which was discussed on Saturday and is being discussed again today. I find it difficult to follow the reasoning adopted by the members of the government in bringing this report to parliament in this manner. In the first place, I feel that this point has not been seriously considered in any way, shape or form by any of the subcommittees. Of course we all recognize the fact that when it came to the general committee only on Saturday it was simply impossible for them to give this matter the consideration a question of this importance deserves.
This is a measure of extreme importance to the people of Canada. With the many constituencies across this country which are vitally concerned by the action of this government, and with this matter being brought to this parliament in the dying days of this session, when the heat of this July weather is driving us from this chamber and when members are anxious to get home, I feel that we simply cannot give this matter the thorough discussion we should give it at this time. It is most unfortunate that the government have decided to rush this legislation through, because there could have been ample time to discuss this matter. It was first mentioned in the speech from the throne back in February. I think the resolution was presented to parliament on March 10. We have had almost four months to study this matter. Then they bring the matter before parliament on the first day of July, a day later than we intended to adjourn.
I feel that the government will regret exceedingly the fact that we have not had time to study thoroughly this extremely important matter, and to give it the analysis and detailed examination that I think it should have. I leave it to every hon. member of this committee to decide whether this is the proper method to deal with matters such as this. In this last minute rush before adjourning, we should have before us the evidence of the subcommittees; we should have the printed report of the general committee. That is something I think is extremely important. We have none of this
[Mr. Laing.l
evidence before us, except what we hear from hon. members. From what we have heard here today, I think it is all the more reason why this matter should not be decided at the present time. If we are going to give intelligent study to and make a thorough analysis of these factors, I feel that this matter should be referred back to the committee for further study. I feel the government will deeply regret the hasty action they have taken at this time.
I will say this, and it is with deep conviction. I feel that the government still have time to reconsider this matter. If they do so, they will only be following the principle established by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier back in 1892 in the redistribution committee set up at that time. I will briefly quote his words. Sir Wilfrid was in the opposition at that time. His words were: the very fact that this measure has been postponed and put off until the dying hours of the session deserves the most severe censure of this house. Those are extremely telling words, Mr. Chairman.
I refer also to the late William Lyon Mackenzie King, who many hon. members of this committee will agree was an outstanding statesman. I quote these gentlemen because I know these two references I have just given are the only ones we can speak of convincingly when we try to get the government to see our point of view on these matters. Mr. Mackenzie King also quoted the same statement in the redistribution committee in 1933; and I might say, Mr. Chairman, that subsequent events have proven the wisdom of his statement at that time. I am sure all hon. members will agree that what has been said by these outstanding leaders should be given serious consideration by hon. members of this committee.
There is another matter which has been dealt with in this committee and which I feel has been most unfair. I also feel that it does not bear the slightest resemblance to what we consider to be good government. I refer to the approach made by the government to the rearrangement of the seats in this House of Commons. When I supported this resolution to set up a committee, I did so because I, along with many other members of the house had, shall we say, sufficient faith and confidence in human nature to think that this committee would bring in a report which we could at least say was brought in without having behind it ulterior motives. I had sufficient faith, as I think all hon. members had, that that would happen. But when we see reports such as those which have been submitted by the subcommittees-particularly from the province of Saskatchewan,

for example-I feel that the faith we had in this committee has crumbled into dust at our feet.
How any committee could bring in a report such as that brought in by the subcommittee for the province of Saskatchewan is beyond anything that any of us, by the widest stretch of the imagination or in the most vivid dreams, could possibly contemplate. I refer, of course, to the mutilation and dissection of the seat of the hon. member for Lake Centre. I think 1 can say without fear of contradiction that the hon. member for Lake Centre is one of the great parliamentarians of this generation who, during the twelve years he has been here in the House of Commons, has given ample evidence of the great ability he possesses. I think we should get down on our knees and thank the Almighty that we have a member in the House of Commons of the type of the hon. member for Lake Centre. Is this the reasoning the people of Canada expected of us as elected representatives of the people? Is this the type of legislation that the 262 constituencies across Canada expect of their representatives in this parliament? In fairness, I ask all hon. members: Is that the type of legislation they expect us to put through? I think it is not. I will say this, that shattered as our thoughts have been by the report of the subcommittee, I do feel that the members of this parliament could not have expected recommendations such as those which have been presented by the subcommittees of the general committee, and particularly the subcommittee from Saskatchewan. God forbid that it should pass. All I can say is that this great institution of parliament, and we as members who comprise this institution, will regret and regret exceedingly what we do in this house if we adopt that report. We shall certainly not be proud of it.
May I again refer to a statement of the late leader of the Liberal party and the former prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, who said at page 5238 of Hansard of May 22, 1933:
I submit that there is no higher trust imposed upon a House of Commons under our constitution than that of justly redistributing the constituencies.
When we think of that statement we wonder how the Manitoba subcommittee in particular could have brought in the recommendation they did, which report deliberately amalgamates two constituencies represented by two very able and outstanding members in this house, the hon. member for Souris and the hon. member for Brandon. This action may be considered by some as smart political manoeuvring, but it certainly is no fine achievement.
Redistribution
I wish, Mr. Chairman, we had the opportunity of producing the reports of the various subcommittees that have been presented, but unfortunately that is denied to us. I should like to say a word concerning the subcommittee for the province of Ontario. We had as our chairman a man whom I have always held and still hold in very high esteem in this house, the hon. member for Ottawa West. May I just digress for a moment. Before coming to this house I, along with many other hon. members, had many opportunities of presiding over meetings of different organizations. That was part of our duties in so many cases, before coming to parliament. Our obligation as chairman of any group was this. When matters of particular interest to any person came up for discussion we always consulted the people who were affected or whose business was under discussion.
Following that line of thought I had hoped that, as has happened from time immemorial, the hon. member for Ottawa West, who was chairman of our subcommittee, would have consulted the hon. member for Haldimand and my colleague the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth on the matter of the amalgamation of our two constituencies. He did not. I regret this exceedingly, because in answer to a question this morning the hon. member for Ottawa West informed us that he consulted different members of the government when it came to questions of changes in their constituencies. For that reason I felt it would have been only common courtesy had he consulted my colleague and myself, particularly when a matter of such consequence as the amalgamation of our two ridings was under discussion. I regret very much that he did not, sir. As I said before, I have great respect for the hon. member for Ottawa West, but I regret that he did not consult us, and more particularly since he admitted this morning that he consulted government members on matters of additions to or subtractions from their ridings. I do not know whether he considered it beneath his dignity or what the reason was, but he did not consult the two members affected in the redistribution of these two ridings.
I should like to ask the members of the government whether the lust for power is so great that they must crush every semblance of opposition in this House of Commons. To me it is regrettable. The actions that have been employed prove beyond any question of doubt that it is the intention of the government to eliminate wherever possible anyone who opposes them in this house. Unfortunately the Prime Minister is not in

Redistribution
his seat. I should like to ask him whether he approves of this kind of action. The Prime Minister is a man of integrity and high principles. I should like to ask him and all hon. members whether they do approve of this sort of thing in this House of Commons to which we are elected to do a job for the people of Canada in an honourable way. The matter of redistribution has been thrown out the window so far as representation by population is concerned. We found that out this afternoon. The hon. member for the Magdalen islands has informed us of the population of the riding which he represents. I am very glad that his riding is maintained. I think he represents that riding well. I do feel, however, if no general principle whatsoever is to be put into effect in the redistribution set-up, then the situation should certainly be corrected.
I do not intend to go into any lengthy discussion, but as a member representing a rural constituency in this parliament of the Dominion of Canada I do feel that this legislation points to a tendency to take away rural representation in this house. I regret that exceedingly. Agriculture is an important industry in Canada. It is one of the primary industries of our country. The whole trend of the report of the redistribution committee is to take away rural representation in this House of Commons.
In conclusion may I say that by some strange methods the Liberal members of this committee have managed to stack the cards against the time-honoured constituency of Haldimand. It is a very historic riding and has been represented in this house ably and well over a period of a hundred years. Hon. members who have read history will recall that William Lyon Mackenzie represented the constituency of Haldimand for four consecutive elections. If a Hansard record of that date had been kept it would show how good a member he was, but he did represent that riding a hundred years ago. Naturally I regret to see Haldimand county being amalgamated, but we must recognize progress and we have to accept these changes.
Certain members of the subcommittee- and I commend them for it-suggested an alternative method under which a portion of a neighbouring constituency could have been associated with Haldimand county. That could have been very effectively carried out, but the members of the committee decided otherwise. My colleague the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth and myself are interested. We do not know yet which one of us will be chosen to contest the constituency, 
but I know he will be very happy to represent the people of Haldimand as I would be happy to represent the residents of his constituency. The remarks I have made, sir, are addressed in all sincerity to the members of the government. I hope they will seriously consider the whole set-up, which is wrong. It is wrong in principle. I think the evidence we have heard here tonight will demonstrate more clearly than any further words I can use that this system should be changed, and that the government should further reconsider the matter. I feel that if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the chairman of the committee, whose responsibility it has been to guide the policy of the committee, will do that he will improve his position in the estimation of the people of Canada to a very great extent.
Mr. Welbourn,: Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a further word in regard to Alberta. It seems to me the subcommittee for that province must have done a fairly good job, because since the orders of the day were called this morning there have been very few references to the Alberta situation.
A little while ago the hon. member for Bow River referred to a principle brought up by my colleague the hon. member for Vegreville. The principle was this, that Calgary should be an urban constituency. That principle was voted on and carried. It was on the motion of opposition members that we added to the urban constituencies so as to take in certain suburbs. I cannot see how that is deviating very much from our original principle. Certainly there is not much difference between the suburbs of a city and the city itself.
In one of our committee meetings the hon. member for Calgary East referred to the community of interest between the Turner valley and the constituency of Calgary East which, as I explained earlier in the day, consists of a narrow corridor through Calgary. I asked him why the community of interest existed between the Turner valley and that particular part of Calgary, rather than all of Calgary, but he could not explain.
The hon. member for Bow River stated also that there were no complaints with respect to what we had proposed in the northern part of the province. Naturally there would be no complaints, because it was Liberal ridings we were carving up in that part of the province. We had to do it because of the shift in population. The hon. member for Bow River is a new member of the committee. We had another member of the Social Credit party on the committee

before, and at one of the meetings that hon. member made the statement that whoever drafted the set-up in Calgary, as it was, was either intoxicated or had ulterior motives. I agree with him.
I would challenge any member or any citizen from the province of Alberta or from any other part of Canada to compare the original map with the map we have now drawn and not say that the one we now have is a much better map.

I do not grasp the meaning of the hon. member's question. Certainly throughout our subcommittee meetings, so far as Alberta was concerned, there was great talk about making a better looking map. But surely that has no significance; it means nothing. The main consideration is whether, in the end, there is a reasonable

arrangement of constituencies, particularly from the point of view of the people voting in those constituencies.
The hon. member for Jasper-Edson made reference to the community of interest which I had mentioned as having existed, and which now exists, between the Turner valley, in which was located the first major oil field in Canada or for that matter in the British empire, and the city of Calgary. I did not say at any time that the community of interest existed solely between that part of Calgary known as Calgary East and the Turner valley. I said there was a community of interest between the Turner valley and Calgary. As it happens, the head offices and the direction of the Turner valley oil field enterprises are almost entirely in the constituency of Calgary East. There can be no doubt that there is a certain community of interest, and in addition to that a large number of the workers in the Turner valley oil fields, as well as those who operate those oil fields, move back and forth between the Turner valley and Calgary.
The hon. member has also said the reason there was no dispute so far as the northern part of the province is concerned was that it is composed entirely of Liberal ridings. That is palpably untrue. As a matter of fact the four constituencies in the north which were merged to form three constituencies consist of one which is now held by a Liberal member-held in the last parliament by a Social Credit member, may I add-and three held in this parliament by Social Credit members, and also held in the last parliament by members of that party. So any suggestion that the changes made in the schedule were made entirely in Liberal ridings, and that therefore there would be no complaint about them, does not hold water.
The chief change was in the elimination of one constituency. Increased representation was allowed to Edmonton because of its increased population. Everyone agreed to that additional seat. Had we acted as some have we might not have agreed to it. We could have said, "Let them go ahead with their increased population, but without any increase in their representation." But the fact is that we did agree to increased representation.
In order to do that a constituency had to be wiped out; and that was a Social Credit constituency, one that has been held by them in the last three parliaments. There can be no argument about that fact. I said this morning and I repeat tonight that I have yet to hear any reasonable argument as to why the general arrangement so far as Calgary seats were concerned should not have been

Redistribution
left as it was. No good argument has been put up, either in the subcommittee or here in the House of Commons, as to why this change should have taken place. On the other hand a reasonable argument has been offered as to why a large number of people will remain convinced that the only reason it was done was some fanciful political reason held by the Liberal political machine in Alberta.

I never for one moment suspected that what I considered to be broadsides in that newspaper article would ever prove true. May I be permitted to quote two paragraphs of that editorial for the edification of the Canadian people and for the enlightenment, if that is still possible, of the government. I quote:
In Canada the redrawing of constituencies before an election is known by the word "redistribution." But there is not too much in a name. For, some years ago, an encyclopaedia of Canada was published in five volumes, under the distinguished editorship of the librarian of the University of Toronto. In this encyclopaedia, "redistribution" is defined with a scholarly exactitude:
"Redistribution, a familiar feature of Canadian political life, is the legislative process whereby the boundaries of electoral constituencies are rearranged prior to an election, in such a way as to improve the chances of the party in power."
Is this not the most lamentable spectacle with which we are now confronted? I had a faint notion of the meaning of gerrymandering at the time I was introduced to the House of Commons, but I was not in the least suspicious that this age-worn political tactic would in 1952 prove so dynamic as to steamroller my concept of democracy in favour of political expediency. I came here somewhat imbued with the theory which was so curtly expressed by the London Free Press in an editorial on April 11, 1952, from which I quote:
The days of political gerrymandering belong to the dark ages of politics.
But to my great stupefaction and surprise I became convinced, after listening to the debate last Saturday and today, that we were indeed being subjected in this redistribution scheme to what has been so aptly described as the law of the jungle; and, as the law of the jungle and the dark ages are two things which in my concept are contemporaneous, if not synonymous-

The shuffling of seats after a census should not be an operation predicated on party voting strength. A readjustment of our representation is a purely technical matter, and should be so treated. In addition to the mathematical factor already referred to, there are others such as the geographical factor, and the ethnic consideration which was referred to for the first time in this debate, I think by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine. These factors, and there may be others, add up, in my opinion, to the broader concept of a proper redistribution, and this is: the adaptability of a proper scheme of representation to present conditions.
From what I have been able to gather from the debate on this bill I am thoroughly convinced that a parliamentary committee is not and never can be the proper body to evolve such a scheme. I am advised-this may be considered hearsay and I do not know whether it is admissible in the house-that a remark such as "who's running this show anyway" has been made by a prominent supporter of the government after a patent example of proposed political carving had been attacked in committee. Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to participate in this debate, but since there has been considerable discussion to do with the constituency of Huron North, and as it affects me in a sense, I believe I should speak for a few moments.
As I understand the schedule now before the committee, it is proposed that there shall be a riding to be known as Huron, which will contain some 44,000 people. That riding will consist of some 20,000 people presently in the riding of Huron North and 24,000 people presently in the riding of Huron-Perth. That means some 76 per cent of the people presently in the riding of Huron North will be in the new riding and some 80 per cent of the people now in Huron-Perth will also be in the new riding. I appreciate the difficulty the committee has had in arriving at an equitable division and in setting proper boundaries for the ridings across Canada. I do not think that task would be any easier even if it were done in another way on another occasion.
Be that as it may, I think the decision with respect to the riding of Huron was made with the intention of taking every possible advantage of the geographical set-up and at the same time avoiding as much as possible the dislocation of existing municipalities. Various references have been made to gerrymandering. Apparently that is the word the opposition uses with reference to the distribution job that has been done, but in this instance I fail to see that it is applicable. In 1945 this riding as it is proposed to be constituted would have provided a Conservative majority of 1,041. In 1949 the majority would have 'been 316. That would seem to be gerrymandering in reverse. Certainly I cannot think it is to the detriment of the hon. member for Huron North.
Reference has been made to the fact that it is proposed to attach the township of Hibbert. The township of Hibbert has been part of Huron-Perth since 1933. That

arrangement was made with the concurrence of the party which receives the support of hon. members opposite. If the job done in 1933 was satisfactory to the party of the hon. member for Huron North, nothing has occurred in the meantime which would indicate that a change should be made.
There is one problem that does cause me concern; that is the situation in rural parts of Ontario created through the mechanization of farming. This mechanization permits the farmers to do a particularly good job with fewer people. This means that in those particular areas the population tends to reduce. If we apply the principle of representation by population this will result in fewer members. I certainly would regret if that trend were permitted to continue to the point where the introduction of policies detrimental to rural Ontario became a political expedient. The fact is that these farmers are continuing to do just as good a job despite their fewer numbers. As a matter of fact the necessity of support governmentwise is greater than ever in view of the increased responsibility that is on the farmers to feed the increasing populations in the cities. Perhaps in this age of floors it would not be unwise to suggest that a floor be created to ensure that the voice of rural Ontario-I speak particularly of Ontario-may always be heard.
When the bill passes, as I anticipate it will, there will be a new riding of Huron in which will be contained some 20,000 residents now in Huron North. I know I speak on behalf of those presently in Huron-Perth when I say that I welcome those citizens of Huron North. Their problems, their outlooks and activities are similar, and I am satisfied that in this new and larger . riding their interests can be represented by the member.
